title: Charging Water by Contact
intro: This lesson examines Cippi of Horus, small magical stelae associated with healing scorpion stings and snakebites. It focuses on how water served as a transfer medium for the carved images and spells.
body:
Cippi of Horus are small magical stelae showing Horus healed of scorpion stings and snakebites. The Brooklyn Museum source, Cippus of Horus on the Crocodiles, belongs to the Late Period - Ptolemaic era. Its recited text includes, "I have recited your incantations, I have conjured with your spells which you created."

In the stated logic of the practice, the object acted as a transfer medium. Liquid poured over the carved surface was believed to absorb the power of the spells and images. The water could then carry that power to someone who drank it or washed with it, so the inscribed spell reached the body through water rather than through hearing.

What is documented ends there: the record describes the method and its underlying belief, not a modern medical effect. Read now, this lesson can be understood as an example of how image, spoken text, object, and liquid were joined into one healing process. It remains uncertain how widely this specific practice was used or how different people understood its results.
reflection: What changes when a written or carved healing text is treated as something that can be carried through water rather than heard directly?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write the recorded phrase in a journal and reflect on how the image of water as a carrier changes its meaning. Do not drink or wash with specially prepared water for healing purposes.
safetyNote: The historical material concerns stings, snakebites, drinking, and washing, but it is recorded here for study and is not a medical treatment. Do not attempt to treat bites, stings, or other injuries with charged water; seek appropriate medical care.
sourceCitation: Cippus of Horus, Brooklyn Museum - Brooklyn Museum, Cippus of Horus on the Crocodiles

title: Guarding Children
intro: This lesson compares two protective approaches for an infant in the Berlin papyrus: a spoken barrier against a stealthy demon and a physical cord amulet. The entry concerns spells 65 and 68 as cited in Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts.
body:
The source records a protection against a demon that enters stealthily. It lists clover, garlic, and honey among the protective substances, and it also gives a spell for a knotted cord tied at a baby's throat. The two approaches are presented in spells 65 and 68 of the Berlin papyrus.

In its own terms, the spoken approach creates a barrier by addressing a named intruder. The physical approach uses a flax cord made with seven knots and placed at the infant's throat. Together, they show protection as both spoken action and a material object kept on the child.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can be understood as a study of how protection was expressed through words, substances, and a wearable cord. The record does not explain how the substances were prepared, how the cord was made in detail, or why the number seven was selected, so those points remain uncertain.
reflection: How does the contrast between naming an intruder aloud and placing a seven-knotted cord on an infant shape your understanding of protection in this text?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry aloud and write two brief notes: one describing the spoken barrier, and one describing the flax cord with seven knots. Do not attempt to recreate the historical procedure.
safetyNote: Because the historical material involves an infant, plants, and a cord tied at a baby's throat, it is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Do not use the listed substances medicinally or place cords around a child's neck.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 65 (Papyrus Berlin 3027, recto 2, 2-7) and spell 68

title: Handbooks, Not Scripture
intro: This lesson examines the London Medical Papyrus as a working handbook rather than a sacred book. It shows how medical material could be collected for practical use in ancient Egypt.
body:
The London Medical Papyrus, British Museum EA 10059, dates to about 1325 BC. It contains nineteen pages and sixty-one paragraphs, with incantations numbered 1 to 52 across the recto and verso: numbers 1 to 33 in columns 1 to 11, and numbers 34 to 52 in columns 12 to 19.

Its form suggests a compilation copied for use rather than composed as a sacred book. A handbook could gather material that its owner found effective, so duplicate cures, foreign-language charms, and unrelated recipes could appear side by side without contradiction. Practical usefulness, not uniform arrangement, held the collection together.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this papyrus invites attention to the difference between an organized doctrine and a working collection of remedies and charms. The record does not explain how each item was selected, or how every item was used in practice, so those details remain uncertain. This is a historical lesson in reading a manuscript on its own terms, not a modern prescription.
reflection: How might reading the London Medical Papyrus as a working collection, rather than as a single consistent doctrine, change the way you understand its duplicate cures and unrelated recipes?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the description of the London Medical Papyrus and make two short lists: what the record documents, and what it leaves uncertain. Do not treat any historical medical material as a modern prescription.
safetyNote: The historical material is recorded for study and is not a modern prescription. Do not attempt historical medical procedures based on this entry.
sourceCitation: London Medical Papyrus (BM EA 10059) - British Museum EA 10059: columns 1-11 (incantations 1-33) recto, 12-19 (34-52) verso

title: Healing Statues and Cippi
intro: This lesson examines Egyptian healing statues and cippi, including Cairo JE 69771 and the Cippus of Horus on the Crocodiles. Their inscribed spells could be used as both public texts and healing objects.
body:
Alongside papyri, Egyptians used inscribed stone for healing. The record names healing statues such as Cairo JE 69771 and cippi showing Horus cured of stings. The cited material includes Borghouts spells 87 and 142 and the Brooklyn Museum's Cippus of Horus on the Crocodiles.

These objects combined written instruction with a physical means of use. Liquid was poured over the carved spells, and the liquid was believed to carry the power of the words. The same text known from a papyrus could be cut into stone, allowing people to obtain it without a literate practitioner.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this practice shows how inscription, healing, and access were joined in one object within its own historical terms. It also invites attention to the difference between a text that records a belief and a modern medical treatment. What remains uncertain is how each person used or understood these objects in daily life. The record identifies their purpose and logic, but it does not provide a modern prescription.
reflection: What changes when a healing text is made into a public stone object that people can approach without a literate practitioner?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the description of a healing statue or cippus and journal about how its words and physical form work together. This is for historical reflection, not a reconstruction of the rite or a medical treatment.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. These objects are not modern medical prescriptions; seek appropriate medical care for illness, bites, or stings.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts; Brooklyn Museum - Borghouts spells 87 and 142 (healing statue Cairo JE 69771); Brooklyn Museum, Cippus of Horus on the Crocodiles

title: Heka: Magic as a God
intro: This lesson examines Heka, the personification of magic in Ancient Egyptian religious thought. The Metternich Stela presents Heka as a divine agent within a group of gods protecting against a crocodile.
body:
The Metternich Stela, from the 30th Dynasty, records a water-protection spell involving four great gods: the Sun, Sekhmet, Thoth, and Heka. In the account, the gods disable a crocodile. One of the stated acts is that "your eyes have been blinded by Magic," with Heka named as the divine agent.

Within this religious framework, magic was not merely a human technique or an outside force. Magic itself belonged to the pantheon and could act as a god. This explains why the text can present prayer and spell together without treating them as opposing practices.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson presents Heka as a way to understand how Egyptian theology joined divine power and protective speech. The record does not explain beyond this passage how worshippers understood Heka in every setting, so broader interpretations remain uncertain. The central point is that magic was treated as a divine presence within the religious order, not as something separate from it.
reflection: How does viewing magic as a divine being, rather than only as a human technique, change the way you understand the relationship between prayer and protection in this text?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the lesson aloud and journal one paragraph about how a tradition might change when it treats an abstract force as a divine presence. This is reflection, not a reconstruction of the historical spell.
safetyNote: The source text includes a crocodile in a protective account. Keep this lesson as study only, and do not approach, handle, or interfere with animals.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela, section I (the Sun, Sekhmet, Thoth and Heka)

title: Isis, Mistress of Magic
intro: This lesson explores Isis as a central magical figure in Ancient Egyptian healing texts. It focuses on healing through the telling of a myth with a known outcome.
body:
Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts, and the Metternich Stela present Isis in healing material from the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC. The record describes her as the lady of words of power, recounts her negotiation with Re for her poisoned child, and preserves the narrative of the seven scorpions as a standard cure. The cited material includes Borghouts spells 90 and 91 and the Metternich Stela 108-251.

In its own terms, the healing did not depend only on a short formula. The practitioner recited a story in which a divine danger had already been faced and overcome. By placing the patient within that narrative, the spell connected the present illness to a case whose outcome was already known: healing.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this material can be studied as an example of how myth, divine authority, and spoken words were joined in an ancient healing text. Its specific historical use and the extent to which every element was understood as literal, symbolic, or both remain uncertain from this record alone. The practice note identifies this as a historical reconstruction for study, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What changes when healing is understood through a story of Isis overcoming danger rather than through a standalone formula?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the lesson aloud once, then write a short journal entry about how the story of a known recovery affects your understanding of healing. This is reflection, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical material includes poisoning, stings, and healing claims. It is recorded for study and must not be attempted as a medical procedure or used in place of appropriate care.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts; Metternich Stela - Borghouts spells 90 and 91 (P. Chester Beatty VII recto 5, 4-7; Metternich Stela 108-251)

title: Knots as Working Technology
intro: This lesson examines knotted cords as part of a healing procedure in Ancient Egyptian magical texts. The practice is recorded in Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts, in spells 42 and 43.
body:
The source records strips of fabric fitted with seven knots and applied to the body. A conjuration for an aching head was tied to the sufferer, making the cord part of the treatment. The material belongs to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC, and is identified as Ancient Egyptian.

In its own terms, the knot gave the spoken work a physical form. The recitation and the cord operated together, while the act of tying held the spell in place on the body. Binding was therefore not only an image or description; it was also a practical way to carry and fix the working.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can show how words, objects, and bodily application were joined in one historical healing method. It does not establish that the method treated headaches, and its effectiveness remains uncertain. The record is useful for studying the logic of the rite, not for supplying a modern medical treatment.
reflection: What changes in your understanding of a spoken healing formula when you consider the cord and its knots as part of the treatment rather than as separate objects?
practice: As a modern study practice, tie seven ordinary knots in a piece of cord while reading the entry aloud, then untie them and note what the physical sequence adds to your understanding. This is not a reconstruction of the historical rite or a medical treatment.
safetyNote: The historical material concerns healing and bodily application. It is recorded for study and is not a modern prescription; do not use a knotted cord to treat an illness or delay appropriate medical care.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 42 (P. Leiden I 348, recto 2, 9-3, 3) and spell 43 (recto 1, 6-10)

title: Medicine and Magic Were One Practice
intro: This lesson examines the London Medical Papyrus, an Ancient Egyptian healing text from around 1325 BC. It records medical and magical material together, covering skin and eye complaints, bleeding, and burns.
body:
The London Medical Papyrus, also called BM EA 10059, contains 19 pages and 61 paragraphs. Of these, 25 are medical, while the remaining material is magical. Incantations 1 to 52 appear across the recto and verso and address healing concerns including skin and eye complaints, bleeding, and burns.

In its own terms, illness could be attributed to hostile spirits. A treatment therefore included both a prescription and the words spoken over it. The scribe who recorded the dressing also recorded the accompanying charm, treating practical care and spoken magic as parts of one treatment rather than as separate categories.

What is documented ends there: the papyrus shows that medicine and magic shared the same healing practice, but it does not establish how effective each part was. Read now, this challenges the habit of dividing ancient healing into real medicine and superstition. It also shows how the categories used by a modern reader may differ from those used by the text's scribe.
reflection: What might be overlooked when a healing text is divided into medical instructions and magical words instead of being read as one combined practice?
practice: As a modern practice, read the lesson aloud and journal about how your own ideas about healing separate physical care, words, and belief. This is reflection only, not a reconstruction of an Egyptian treatment.
safetyNote: The medical procedures and healing claims in this historical text are recorded for study and must not be attempted. For illness, bleeding, burns, or other health concerns, seek appropriate modern medical care.
sourceCitation: London Medical Papyrus (BM EA 10059) - London Medical Papyrus, 19 pages, 61 paragraphs, incantations 1-52 across recto and verso

title: Naming the Body Part by Part
intro: This lesson examines an Egyptian protective spell that names the body part by part and assigns each part a divine owner. The same listing approach also appears in a cat spell.
body:
The Metternich Stela records an Egyptian protective sequence for the body, moving through the head, eye, nose, arms, chest, belly, thighs, shins, and feet. The subject is linked with gods as the spell proceeds. A related cat spell uses the same approach for the animal's limbs. These materials are cited in the Metternich Stela section G and Borghouts spell 87.

In its own terms, the sequence works by making every part known and protected. Once each limb has a divine owner, no part is left unclaimed for poison to occupy. The ordered list is therefore not just a description of the body. It presents complete coverage as the basis of protection.

What is documented ends there: the texts record the body-by-body structure and its protective reasoning. Read now, this can be understood as a focused way to notice the whole body rather than treating danger as something vague or separate from particular places. What remains uncertain is how every ancient reader or practitioner understood the relationship between each body part and its divine owner. This lesson is a study of the historical text, not a modern medical prescription.
reflection: When you move through the body from head to feet, which parts are easiest to overlook, and what does the complete sequence make you notice?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the body sequence slowly and write down each part in order. Notice whether naming every part changes your sense of completeness or attention.
safetyNote: The historical material refers to poison and a healing statue, but it is recorded for study and is not a modern prescription. Do not use the spell in place of medical care.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela; Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Metternich Stela section G; Borghouts spell 87 (healing statue Cairo JE 69771, 112-180)

title: Nine Tablets, One Night
intro: This lesson examines the structure of the Maqlu series, an Akkadian or Standard Babylonian corpus from the 1st millennium BC. Its nine tablets separate spoken incantations from the ritual sequence that accompanied them.
body:
The Maqlu series runs to nine tablets. Eight tablets preserve the texts of nearly a hundred incantations. The ninth, called the ritual tablet, gives the opening lines in order and adds brief notes about the actions that accompany them.

The corpus therefore has two connected layers. The incantation tablets record what was said, while the ritual tablet records what was done and the sequence in which it was done. In its own terms, the complete working of the corpus depended on keeping speech and action together rather than treating either layer as sufficient by itself.

What is documented ends there: this entry records the arrangement of the tablets and their different kinds of information, not a full account of every action or incantation. Read now, the structure offers a disciplined way to study a complex ritual text by separating words from procedure and then comparing them. It remains uncertain from this record how the brief notes relate to every one of the nearly hundred incantations, or how the complete sequence was carried out in practice.
reflection: When studying a ritual text, what might be gained or lost by separating the words spoken from the actions performed?
practice: As a modern study practice, read a short passage from a historical text and make two columns in your notes: one for what is said and one for what is done. This is an organizational exercise, not a reconstruction of the rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu series - Maqlu, eight incantation tablets plus ritual tablet (Tablet IX)

title: Protecting the House Itself
intro: This lesson examines an Ancient Egyptian house-protection spell recorded in the Chester Beatty material. It presents the dwelling piece by piece, giving protective significance to its openings, structures, and private spaces.
body:
Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts records this as spell 11 in P. Chester Beatty VIII, verso 1, 1-2, 4. The text belongs to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC, and is described as a spell concerning the protection of a house from a hostile dead person.

The spell surveys the house by naming features such as the window, chink, bolts, hole, hiding place, cross timbers, room, and bed. Each part is assigned a protective power. Its logic is comprehensive: by listing possible openings and important spaces, the text treats the whole structure as something that can be secured piece by piece.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be understood as a lesson in noticing how safety is imagined through careful attention to the details of a home. The record does not explain every protective power or describe a modern application, so the exact meaning of each feature remains uncertain. Its surviving outline nevertheless shows a deliberate connection between architecture, vulnerability, and protection.
reflection: Which overlooked feature of your own home would you include first in a careful survey of its openings and private spaces?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the historical rite, walk through your home and make a written list of its doors, windows, gaps, locks, and resting spaces. Note one ordinary, practical way each area is maintained or secured.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 11 (P. Chester Beatty VIII, verso 1, 1-2, 4)

title: Saying It Again: Three and Seven
intro: This lesson examines prescribed repetition in Mesopotamian and Egyptian magical texts. The records distinguish between three-fold, seven-fold, and four-fold recitation.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records an instruction for an incantation to be recited three times. The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden most often specifies seven repetitions, and sometimes four. Seven-fold recitation appears throughout the handbook, while four-fold repetition is described as standard in Egyptian healing spells.

In these sources, the number of repetitions was part of the procedure rather than a choice left to the practitioner. The instruction was to follow the stated count, whether three, seven, or four. Repetition was therefore prescribed and not improvised, placing the spoken act within the form given by the text.

What is documented ends there: the records establish the counts and their use, but do not state here why each number was selected. What remains uncertain is the reasoning practitioners attached to the different counts, since this entry does not provide an explanation. Read now, the lesson can encourage careful attention to an instruction without treating historical reconstruction as a modern prescription.
reflection: When you follow a written instruction, how does knowing that its repetition count was prescribed rather than improvised change the way you read it?
practice: As a modern study practice, choose a short passage from your notes and read it aloud three times, then seven times on another occasion. Notice how the fixed count changes your attention; this is not a reconstruction of the historical rites.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet; Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 6'-8'; P. London-Leiden, col. III, 14-16

title: Spells for Bad Dreams
intro: This lesson examines two Ancient Egyptian spells for bad dreams. The records pair spoken recitation with bread, herbs steeped in beer and myrrh, and rubbing the face after waking.
body:
Borghouts records one spell for a man who has a nightmare in his own place and another related spell in Ancient Egyptian magical texts. The sources are spell 7 in P. Chester Beatty III and spell 8 in P. Chester Beatty VI, from the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC.

Egyptian practitioners treated nightmares as an attack to be answered. The remedy combined speech with food, a preparation of herbs steeped in beer and myrrh, and touch through rubbing the face. Its focus was the dreamer's body on waking, rather than an explanation of the dream's content.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson draws attention to how words, nourishment, and physical contact were joined in a response to distress. It can also prompt reflection on how waking actions may help someone feel reoriented after a frightening dream. The record does not establish how often these spells were used or how practitioners judged their success, and those points remain uncertain.
reflection: When you wake from a frightening dream, which part of a response feels most grounding to you: spoken words, nourishment, or gentle physical contact?
practice: As a modern practice, write a short reassuring sentence to read when you wake from a bad dream, then note what you remember about the dream and how your body feels. This is a reflective exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Do not ingest the described preparations or use named plants medicinally.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 7 (P. Chester Beatty III, recto 10, 6-9); spell 8 (P. Chester Beatty VI, verso 2, 5-9)

title: Spells for Childbirth
intro: This lesson examines childbirth spells preserved in Papyrus Berlin 3027. The spells use the successful delivery of Isis or Hathor as a mythic precedent for a labouring woman.
body:
Borghouts records these spells as spells 61-63 in Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts, from Papyrus Berlin 3027. They belong to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC, and include recitations of the delivery of Isis or Hathor. One spell threatens that heaven, earth, and the inundation will cease if the birth does not proceed.

In the terms of the spells, the mythic parallel was the mechanism. The labouring woman was identified with a goddess whose birth was already known to have succeeded. Repeating that precedent presented her delivery as part of an established divine event, while the threat of cosmic collapse pressed the birth toward completion.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this material shows how divine precedent could give childbirth a sacred structure and express urgency through cosmic imagery. It remains uncertain from this record how these spells were used in individual births or how effective practitioners believed each form to be.
reflection: What might change in your understanding of childbirth when a difficult human event is framed through the already successful birth of a goddess?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write a short reflection on the kinds of stories or precedents that help people feel supported during difficult transitions. Do not treat the historical spell as medical guidance.
safetyNote: The historical material is recorded for study and must not be attempted. It is not a modern medical prescription; seek qualified medical care for childbirth.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spells 61-63 (Papyrus Berlin 3027, recto 1, 9-2, 10; verso 3, 8-4, 3)

title: The Harris Magical Papyrus
intro: This lesson examines the Harris Magical Papyrus, an Ancient Egyptian compilation of hymns and incantations concerned mainly with crocodiles and other dangerous animals. It also introduces the manuscript history and the systems used to cite its surviving sections.
body:
BM EA 10042 comes from Deir el-Medina on the Theban west bank and dates to the 20th Dynasty, c. 1186-1069 BC. It was a compilation of hymns and incantations, with material aimed mainly at crocodiles on the recto and at other dangerous animals on the verso. Of nine original recto pages and three verso pages, six recto pages and part of one verso page survive.

In its own terms, the text worked through hymns and incantations directed toward animal dangers. The surviving arrangement distinguishes crocodile material from the material about other dangerous animals, suggesting that the threats were addressed through organized written and spoken formulas. The record does not preserve enough detail here to explain the exact actions, words, or expected results of each passage.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this papyrus can be studied as a record of how danger from animals was framed in an Ancient Egyptian magical compilation, without treating it as a complete surviving ritual. The surviving text is incomplete, and the exact working logic of individual sections remains uncertain. For study, cite sections by Lange's lettered divisions A-Z, which skip J and W; relevant editions include Chabas 1860, Lange 1927, and Leitz 1999. Fragments are also held in Heidelberg under inventory 24475.
reflection: How does knowing that the papyrus survives only in fragments change the way you understand its treatment of crocodiles and other dangerous animals?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry aloud and make a short journal note distinguishing what the record documents from what remains uncertain. You may also copy the citation system A-Z, noting that J and W are skipped.
safetyNote: The historical material involves dangerous animals and is recorded for study; it must not be attempted or reconstructed. Do not approach, handle, feed, or provoke crocodiles or other dangerous animals.
sourceCitation: Harris Magical Papyrus (BM EA 10042) - British Museum EA 10042; Lange 1927; Science in Ancient Egypt record

title: The Number Seven in Egyptian Practice
intro: This lesson examines the repeated use of the number seven in Ancient Egyptian magical texts. It focuses on seven as a sign of completeness in knots, arranged objects, recitations, and the scorpions accompanying Isis.
body:
In Egyptian magical practice, seven appears in several recorded forms. The texts describe seven knots in a cord, seven clean loaves and seven lumps of salt placed around a divination vessel, seven bricks, and seven scorpions accompanying Isis. These examples are found in Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts and the P. London-Leiden, from the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC.

Within the terms of these practices, the number marked a complete working. It governed how many knots were tied, how many objects were arranged around a vessel, and how many times words were recited. The repeated count gave the action a defined structure.

What is documented ends there: the sources show where seven occurs, but they do not fully explain one single meaning for every example. Read now, this pattern can be studied as a way of noticing how number, order, and repetition shaped a magical working. Whether seven always carried the same force across these practices remains uncertain or debated.
reflection: When you notice seven in a ritual or repeated action, what changes for you when you treat it as a sign of completeness rather than merely a quantity?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the historical rites, arrange seven ordinary objects in a row and write one sentence about how the fixed number changes your attention. Put the objects away when you are finished.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts; P. London-Leiden - Borghouts spells 42, 43, 68; P. London-Leiden col. III, 5-13

title: The Patient Speaks in First Person
intro: This lesson examines how the Maqlu incantations use the sufferer's own voice. It focuses on grammar, agency, and the role of first-person speech in the ritual's structure.
body:
The Maqlu incantations are preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts and occur across tablets I-VIII. Almost every incantation is written in the sufferer's voice, using statements such as "I call upon you," "I am raising the torch," and "my witch, my deceiver." The record presents the afflicted person as the speaker of the case.

In its own terms, the ritual worked through a first-person defence. The patient stated the situation aloud rather than simply receiving words from the exorcist. This structure continues into the closing act, in which the patient recognises his own reflection rather than receiving a blessing from the exorcist.

What is documented ends there: the grammar and structure show that the sufferer speaks and takes an active role. Read now, this can be understood as a lesson in how ritual language gives form to personal agency. It remains uncertain how every historical participant understood the patient's reflection or how consistently this pattern was carried out in practice.
reflection: What changes when a person states their own case aloud instead of waiting for someone else to speak on their behalf?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, write three first-person sentences describing a difficulty you are facing and what you want to understand about it. Read them aloud as an exercise in noticing your own voice, not as a reconstruction of the Maqlu rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, incantation incipits across tablets I-VIII

title: The Plague of the Year
intro: This lesson examines a group of protective spells on the verso of the Edwin Smith papyrus. The spells address the breath of the plague of the year and the destructive forces associated with Sakhmet.
body:
The spells are recorded as Borghouts spells 14-16 in the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, 18, 2-19. They belong to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC, and are described as wards against the breath of the plague of the year, as well as the murderers and incendiaries of Sakhmet, the goddess who sends epidemic disease.

In its own terms, the threat was seasonal and atmospheric. It was understood as something that could travel through breath and wind, so protection was not limited to the body. The countermeasures included perimeter actions, such as walking the round of the house, creating a protective boundary around the place at risk.

What is documented ends there: the record preserves the spells and their protective framing, but it does not establish how effective they were or how every action was performed. Read now, this material can show how seasonal danger was given a shape that people could respond to through movement and attention to household boundaries. The historical logic connects an unseen threat with a visible circuit around the home.
reflection: How might the seasonal and atmospheric framing of this threat have shaped the way a household understood its boundaries and responsibilities?
practice: As a modern practice, take a calm walk around your home while noticing doors, windows, and other boundaries, then write down what helps you feel prepared for seasonal illness. This is a reflective exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical spells are recorded for study and are not a treatment or prevention for epidemic disease. For health concerns, use current public health guidance and seek professional medical care.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spells 14-16 (Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, 18, 2-19)

title: The Three Movements of the Night
intro: This lesson follows the changing structure of Maqlu, an Akkadian and Standard Babylonian text from the 1st millennium BC. Its three ritual sequences move from destructive action against the source of harm toward purification, care, and protection for the patient.
body:
Maqlu's first, second, and third ritual sequences describe a night divided into three movements. Tablets I-IV focus on destructive rites directed against the source of the harm. Tablets V-VII shift attention to fumigating the house and treating the patient. In the last hours come washing, a dawn invocation, and self-recognition in water.

In its own terms, the sequence gives the work a changing direction. At first, attention is placed on attacking or removing the source of harm. As the night continues, the house and patient become the focus. Purification, washing, invocation, and recognition in water complete the movement toward future protection.

What is documented ends there: the text records an arc from attack to care, not a modern therapeutic method. Read now, this structure can be understood as a movement away from fixation on an enemy and toward restoring the patient's condition and sense of protection. It remains uncertain how every stage was understood or carried out in practice, because this record does not provide those details.
reflection: When a response to harm moves from attacking its source toward caring for the patient and protecting the future, what changes in your own attention?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write three short lines labeled release, care, and protection. Under each label, note one safe action or intention for the present day.
safetyNote: The historical material includes fumigating a house. Do not recreate the historical procedure with smoke or flame indoors; use the writing practice instead.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, first, second and third ritual sequences

title: Thoth, the God of Spells
intro: This lesson examines Thoth as a specialist in ancient Egyptian magical texts. The Metternich Stela presents him as a powerful authority connected with restoring Horus's injured eye and dealing with poison.
body:
The Metternich Stela describes Thoth arriving in spell after spell from the sky at the Sun's command. It records that he restores the injured eye of Horus and presents him as arrayed with magic to enchant poison. The cited material also treats Thoth as a recurring specialist within these spells.

In the practitioners' terms, Thoth was more than a deity asked for assistance. He was the professional's patron, the god who wrote and administered spells. When a practitioner says "I am Thoth," the statement claims the authority of the god whose knowledge makes the spell effective.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can highlight the difference between asking a power for help and speaking from an adopted source of authority. The record does not establish exactly how every practitioner understood or performed the phrase "I am Thoth," so its use remains uncertain. Its surviving role is clear enough to show Thoth as a model of specialized magical competence.
reflection: When you speak with authority in your own work, what responsibility should accompany claiming the knowledge or role of a specialist?
practice: As a modern practice, read the lesson aloud and write a short journal entry about the difference between requesting help and speaking with authority. This is a reflection exercise, not a reconstruction of an ancient rite.
safetyNote: The historical material refers to poison, injury, and magical restoration. Treat it as study material only, not as medical guidance or a method for handling poison or treating injuries.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela; The Metropolitan Museum of Art - Metternich Stela sections A, B, G; Stunkel, 'Ancient Egyptian Amulets' (Thoth restores the eye)

title: Treating the Foot to Cure the Head
intro: This lesson examines an Ancient Egyptian healing principle in which a remedy for the head is applied to the lower part of the body. The example comes from the New Kingdom and is recorded in Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts.
body:
Borghouts spell 45 records a conjuration for the head fitted with seven knots and applied to the left foot. The papyrus states plainly that what is applied to the lower part cures the upper part. The related citation is spell 42, from P. Leiden I 348, recto 13, 3-5.

In its own terms, the treatment site did not need to match the location of the complaint. The connection between upper and lower parts allowed a head remedy to be tied to a toe or foot. This principle helps explain why some Egyptian prescriptions appear mismatched to modern readers.

What is documented ends there. The text records the remedy and its stated logic, but it does not establish how the treatment was understood by every practitioner or how effective it was. Read now, the lesson is a reminder to attend to an ancient text's own structure before judging it by modern expectations of bodily treatment. The historical meaning and practical effect of this correspondence remain uncertain.
reflection: What changes when you read the seven-knot remedy according to its own stated connection between the foot and the head rather than by the location of the complaint?
practice: As a modern study practice, write two columns labeled complaint and treatment site, then note how this entry connects the head with the left foot. Use the exercise to observe your assumptions about where a remedy should be applied, not as a medical treatment or reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical material includes a medical claim and is recorded for study. It must not be attempted as a modern prescription; seek qualified medical care for head or other health concerns.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 45 (P. Leiden I 348, recto 13, 3-5); spell 42

title: Water Closes What Fire Opened
intro: This lesson examines the closing water rites described in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. Tablets VII and VIII contain a series of short handwashing formulas recited as dawn breaks.
body:
The cited passage from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a transition from fire to water. After the burning, the fire is quenched, the house is sprinkled, and the rite continues with repeated fresh washings. The handwashing series appears in Tablets VII and VIII, including the lines cited from obv. 148'-161'.

The formulas mark the coming of morning with phrases such as Dawn has broken and It is morning, yea morning. Each washing is paired with a short spoken formula, including I wash my hands. Within the rite's own structure, water follows fire as the concluding action, bringing the ceremony into the dawn and emphasizing repeated purification.

What is documented ends with this series of handwashings and its dawn setting. Read now, this passage can be understood as a carefully ordered movement from intense ritual action toward cleansing and closure. It remains uncertain how every individual washing was performed or how participants understood each separate formula beyond the sequence recorded here.
reflection: What changes in your understanding of ritual closure when you follow the movement from fire, to sprinkling, to repeated handwashing at dawn?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, wash your hands slowly at the start of the day and notice the transition from sleep into morning. You may read the recorded phrases silently as a study prompt.
safetyNote: The historical material includes burning and fire quenching. It is presented here for study; do not recreate the fire-based ritual.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 148'-161' (handwashing series)

title: Wedjat Eye and Heart Scarab
intro: This lesson compares the wedjat amulet with the heart scarab and other Egyptian amulets. It also distinguishes objects used by the living and dead from those intended only for funerary use.
body:
The wedjat shows the healed eye of Horus, injured or stolen by Seth and restored by Thoth. It combines a human eye with a falcon eye and was used for both living and dead. The heart scarab was used to secure a favourable verdict when the heart was weighed against maat. Heart scarabs, headrests, and the Late Period two-finger amulet were strictly funerary. Textual amulets were spells written on linen or papyrus, then folded and strung.

In its own terms, the wedjat carried the power of a restored injury and transferred regeneration to its wearer. The heart scarab addressed the judgement of the dead, seeking a favourable result in the weighing of the heart against maat. These objects therefore served different audiences and purposes, even though both belonged to the wider practice of amulets.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can prompt reflection on the difference between healing imagery, protection, and preparation for death. The historical record here does not establish how every wearer understood these objects or how consistently their intended effects were believed to work.
reflection: How does separating the wedjat from strictly funerary amulets change your understanding of what protection meant for the living and the dead?
practice: As a modern practice, write two short notes: one about a past difficulty you hope to recover from, and one about a value you want to keep in view when making a difficult choice. This is reflection, not a reconstruction of an ancient rite.
safetyNote: The museum essay is used as a factual reference. Verify reuse terms with the Metropolitan Museum of Art before quoting its text or reproducing images in the app.
sourceCitation: Isabel Stunkel, 'Ancient Egyptian Amulets', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2019)

title: What Maqlu Was
intro: This lesson introduces Maqlu, a Babylonian anti-witchcraft ritual whose name means "Burning." It presents the work as a single movement from danger and bondage toward life, purification, freedom, and the return of harm to its source.
body:
Maqlu is the most extensive Babylonian anti-witchcraft ritual known. It belongs to the Mesopotamian tradition and is written in Akkadian, in Standard Babylonian. The overview is recorded in the Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals and discussed by Schwemer in the Maqlu overview from 2014.

In its own terms, Maqlu is not a random collection of charms. Its sections follow one connected argument. The victim moves from imminent death back to life, is purified, is released from what binds them, and is protected by returning the harm to whoever sent it. Each part supports this larger transition.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this structure can be understood as a study in reversal: a condition of danger is changed step by step into life and freedom. The precise performance of every section remains uncertain from this overview, so the lesson does not reconstruct individual acts or words. Its clearest teaching is the ritual's overall shape: death to life, bound to free, and harm returned to its author.
reflection: What changes when Maqlu is studied as one movement from danger to freedom rather than as a collection of separate charms?
practice: As a modern study practice, write the sequence "death to life, bound to free, harm returned" in a journal and reflect on what each transition means to you. This is a reflection exercise, not a reconstruction of Maqlu.
safetyNote: The historical title refers to "Burning." Do not attempt to reconstruct any historical rite involving fire; this entry is for study only.
sourceCitation: Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals (CMAwRo) - Schwemer, Maqlu overview, CMAwRo (2014)

title: Where an Amulet's Power Came From
intro: This lesson examines where an ancient Egyptian amulet was understood to gain its force. Its power was associated with several features of the object and with actions performed around it, not only with its visible image.
body:
Ancient Egyptian amulets drew force from seven connected factors: shape, decoration, inscription, colour, material, words spoken over the object, and acts performed with it. The source records that, in principle, anything could become an amulet through a magical act.

This system treated the object as more than a picture or ornament. Green and blue faience was favoured because it was linked to life and regeneration. Red represented dangerous forces, so the colour could also be protective in itself. The material, colours, markings, spoken words, and actions all contributed to the amulet's purpose.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this account encourages attention to how meaning can be built through several details at once, rather than assigned only by an image. The record does not explain exactly how each factor was combined in every individual amulet, so the precise working of particular examples remains uncertain. For study, the seven factors provide a careful way to describe an object without reducing it to its shape alone.
reflection: When you look at an object today, which of its seven recorded features most strongly shapes the meaning you give it, and why?
practice: As a modern study practice, choose an ordinary object and write seven notes about its shape, decoration, inscription if any, colour, material, words associated with it, and actions connected with it. This is observation and journalling, not a reconstruction of an ancient rite.
safetyNote: The museum essay is used as a factual reference. Verify reuse terms with the Metropolitan Museum of Art before quoting its text or reproducing images in the app.
sourceCitation: Isabel Stunkel, 'Ancient Egyptian Amulets', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2019)

title: Who Actually Performed the Ritual
intro: This lesson examines who performed a Maqlu anti-witchcraft ritual and how the roles of specialist and patient were divided. The ritual was carried out by a trained asipu, or exorcist, rather than by the sufferer alone.
body:
The Maqlu material records a trained professional, the asipu or exorcist, as the person who ran the ritual. The sufferer did not independently perform the whole ceremony. Instead, the text presents distinct responsibilities for the specialist and the patient.

The asipu prepared and handled the ritual work, protected the crucible with a magic circle, managed the fire, and directed the recitations. The patient spoke the words and was washed. These instructions show that the ritual depended on coordinated roles rather than on one person carrying out every action.

What is documented ends there: the record explains the division of roles, but it does not establish every practical detail of how each task was carried out. Read now, this distinction helps prevent modern readers from collapsing the specialist and patient into a single role. What remains uncertain is how consistently this arrangement was followed in every performance. The entry is therefore best read as a study of ritual organization, not as a modern procedure.
reflection: How does separating the asipu's handling of the ritual from the patient's speaking and washing change your understanding of responsibility in Maqlu?
practice: As a modern study practice, write two brief columns labeled specialist and patient, then place only the recorded actions under each heading. This is an exercise in reading the roles clearly, not a reconstruction of the rite.
sourceCitation: Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals - Schwemer, Maqlu overview: role of the exorcist

title: Why It Is Called Burning
intro: This lesson uses the title Maqlu, meaning "Burning," as a key to understanding the structure of the series. Its first half of the night centers on a crucible in which images of sorcerers are destroyed by fire.
body:
The Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals records Maqlu as a series whose name means "Burning." The overview identifies the first half of the night as being organized around a crucible, with images of the sorcerers destroyed by fire.

Within the ritual's own terms, burning is not a minor detail but the central action. The fire provides the structure for the opening part of the night, and the destruction of the images gives the rite its main movement. When a passage refers to burning, melting, or extinguishing, those actions help show where the text is within its larger sequence.

What is documented ends there: the title and the role of burning in the ritual's structure. Read now, this can serve as a reading method rather than a modern instruction, directing attention to what is being destroyed and how the text marks that change. The record does not explain every passage or settle all questions about how each action was understood.
reflection: How does reading Maqlu through its central image of burning change your sense of what the text is doing from one passage to the next?
practice: As a modern study practice, read a short passage from your materials and journal every reference to something being burned, melted, or extinguished. Note how each image seems to organize your understanding of the passage, without attempting to recreate the rite.
safetyNote: The historical material involves fire. Treat it as a text for study only, and do not attempt to recreate its burning rites or use flame as part of this exercise.
sourceCitation: Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals - Schwemer, Maqlu overview: the name and the burning rites

title: Why Scorpions and Snakes Dominate
intro: This lesson examines why surviving Egyptian magical texts so often address scorpions, snakes, crocodiles, and dogs. Their frequency provides evidence about the dangers that mattered in everyday life.
body:
Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts records spells addressing stings and bites, including spells 87, 90, 91, 104-113, 121, 137, and 142. The dangers named include scorpions, snakes, crocodiles, and dogs. The material belongs to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC.

The surviving pattern suggests that these texts focused on everyday lethal risks that medicine could least control. Their attention was directed toward hazards found in fields, along riverbanks, and in bedrooms, rather than mainly toward grand cosmic ambitions. In this setting, magical writing addressed immediate threats to human safety.

What is documented ends there: the frequency of these spells is useful social evidence, but the record does not provide the details of a particular rite or explain how each practitioner understood its effectiveness. It remains uncertain how widely these texts were used in daily life or how their users judged their success. Read now, this collection shows how the concerns preserved in a corpus can reveal the practical fears of a society.
reflection: What might the prominence of stings and bites change in your picture of what ancient Egyptian people considered urgent or worthy of protection?
practice: As a modern practice, write down the ordinary risks that shape your own daily routines, such as hazards near your home or during travel. Compare that list with the dangers emphasized in this lesson, without attempting to reconstruct any historical procedure.
safetyNote: The historical material concerns animal bites and stings and is recorded for study. It must not be attempted as a medical treatment or as a way to handle or approach animals.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spells 87, 90, 91, 104-113, 121, 137, 142

title: Why the Month of Abu
intro: This lesson examines why the Maqlu ceremony was performed in Abu, roughly July and August. Its timing was connected to beliefs about movement between the world and the netherworld.
body:
The Maqlu records a ceremony performed in the month of Abu, roughly July and August. In the account provided here, this period is associated with the movement of spirits between the world and the netherworld.

Within that understanding, the movement created a particular opportunity. Spirits were believed to be unusually exposed to incantations while passing between these realms. The timing of the ceremony therefore followed the perceived condition of its targets rather than ordinary convenience for the patient.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this example can be understood as a lesson in timing: an action was placed within a calendar period believed to make it more effective. The record does not establish how widely this belief was held or how practitioners judged the spirits' exposure. Its specific teaching is that the month of Abu was treated as a point of access, when ritual words were thought to reach their targets more readily.
reflection: When you choose a time for an important task, what conditions do you believe make it more reachable or effective, and how do those beliefs shape your timing?
practice: As a modern practice, choose one ordinary task and note the time or conditions in which it feels most approachable. Write down what you noticed, without treating the exercise as a reconstruction of the Maqlu ceremony.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, performance in the month of Abu (July/August)

title: An Incantation upon the Assembly of All the Gods
intro: This lesson examines a brief closing formula from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It follows the removal of burned materials and the sprinkling of the house, and addresses the assembly of all the gods rather than a single deity.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records this formula in Akkadian, in the Standard Babylonian tradition. The cited passage is from obv. 94'-95' of manuscripts dating to the 7th century BC. It describes a brief recitation made after the remains had been removed and water had been sprinkled where the burning took place.

The sequence gives the words a closing place within the rite. First, the burning materials and their remains are carried out. Next, the area is sprinkled. Then the speaker says, "I am casting an incantation upon the assembly of all the gods." The wording turns from the completed actions to the full divine assembly, rather than naming one god.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be understood as a study in ritual completion: removal, sprinkling, and a final spoken address form a clear ending. It remains uncertain what precise effect the practitioners expected this brief formula to have, because the record supplies the action and words but no further explanation. Its broad address also invites reflection on how a ritual can conclude by appealing to an entire sacred order.
reflection: What does addressing the entire divine assembly, rather than one god, suggest to you about the meaning of a ritual's final words?
practice: As a modern practice, read the recorded formula aloud once as an act of study, then write a sentence describing how its position after removal and sprinkling shapes its meaning. This is a reflective reading exercise, not a reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical sequence involved burning materials, so it should be treated as a record for study and not recreated. Do not burn materials or attempt the historical procedure.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 94'-95'

title: Back, You Apophis
intro: This lesson examines an Ancient Egyptian confrontation spell against Apophis, the serpent of chaos. It is recorded on the Metternich Stela, dated to the 30th Dynasty, 4th century BC.
body:
The Metternich Stela, in its section titled Spell against Apophis, records commands directed at the serpent. The speaker says, "Back, you Apophis! Withdraw for the Sun!" and declares that Apophis's head has been severed and his form felled with the knife of the great god. The passage also calls on Selket to act through magic.

Within the spell's own logic, speech establishes the serpent's defeat and turns its force away from its intended direction. The command to stop is joined to a request that Selket reverse Apophis's strength through her magic: "Stop, stop! Reverse through her magic!" The words present protection as an accomplished reversal rather than a hoped-for outcome.

What is documented ends there: the record gives the words and their stated magical action, but it does not explain how this particular passage was performed in daily life. Read now, this text can be studied as a focused expression of resistance to chaos, using declarations of defeat and reversal. Whether the spell was understood as literal divine action, ritual speech, or both remains uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: What changes when a threat is addressed as already defeated rather than merely asked to leave?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded phrases silently and journal about how commands of withdrawal and reversal shape the passage. This is a reading exercise, not a reconstruction of the ancient rite.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section C, Spell against Apophis

title: Back, You Fish and Crocodiles
intro: This lesson examines a river-crossing protection spell recorded on the Metternich Stela. The text addresses fish and crocodiles and extends its protective command to the person traveling on the water.
body:
The Metternich Stela, held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art as 50.85, preserves this spell in its section on protection on water. It belongs to the Ancient Egyptian tradition and dates to the 30th Dynasty, in the 4th century BC. The command says, "Back, you fish and crocodiles in the water. Don't lift your face until Osiris has passed by you!" It also orders that the mouth become small and the maw be plugged.

In the spell's own terms, safety is created by commanding the water's inhabitants to withdraw their faces and close their mouths until Osiris has passed. The person actually crossing the water receives the same cover through the stated protection. The language treats spoken authority and the presence of Osiris as a means of controlling danger during travel.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can be understood as a study of how danger on a journey was addressed through direct commands and divine association. It may also invite reflection on the wish to make an uncertain crossing feel ordered and guarded. Whether the words were meant for a specific historical crossing, or how often such a spell was used in practice, remains uncertain from this record.
reflection: When facing an uncertain passage in your own life, what would it mean to name the dangers clearly while also recognizing what remains beyond your control?
practice: As a modern practice, write a short, non-magical travel intention that names the risks you want to respect and the precautions you will take. Read it aloud as a reflection on the historical text, not as a reconstruction or substitute for real water safety.
safetyNote: This entry concerns fish and crocodiles; do not approach, disturb, or attempt to control wildlife. The historical procedure is presented for study and should not be relied on in place of ordinary water-safety precautions.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section I, Spell for protection on water

title: Conjuration for the Head, Four Times
intro: This lesson examines a short Ancient Egyptian head conjuration from the New Kingdom. The text concerns trouble in the head and was recited four times without materials.
body:
Borghouts spell 38 is preserved in P. Leiden I 348, recto 3, 3-5, as recorded in Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts. Dating to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC, it gives a brief conjuration for the head. No materials are specified, and the words are recited four times over the sufferer.

In its own terms, the conjuration addresses the vessels of the eyebrows and the concealed interior of the head. It commands the trouble located there to break out. The working therefore depends on repeated spoken direction, focused on named parts of the head and on expelling the problem from them.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this text can be studied as an example of how a spoken command was used to describe and address bodily distress. The record does not explain what the vessels were understood to be in detail, how the sufferer experienced the rite, or whether it was considered effective. Those points remain uncertain from this entry alone.
reflection: What does the text's focus on the eyebrows and the concealed interior of the head suggest to you about how bodily discomfort was imagined and described?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, write a few sentences about how you describe a headache or other head discomfort in your own words. This is a journaling exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite or a treatment.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted as a treatment. Head pain that is severe, persistent, unusual, or concerning should be discussed with a qualified health professional.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 38 (P. Leiden I 348, recto 3, 3-5)

title: Dawn Has Broken
intro: This lesson presents a short dawn sequence from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It marks the end of a night ritual through spoken formulas and successive handwashings as daylight begins.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a run of very short dawn formulas at obv. 152'-156'. At first light, the sequence says, "Dawn has broken," followed by "It is morning, yea morning" and "At dawn my hands are washed." Each phrase is paired with a fresh handwashing. The manuscripts date to the 7th century BC, and the tradition is Mesopotamian, in Akkadian or Standard Babylonian.

The sequence joins speech, timing, and repeated washing. Its recorded purpose is to close the night ritual and mark passage into daylight, while the handwashing provides an act of purification. The repeated pattern gives the transition a clear order: dawn is announced, morning is affirmed, and the hands are washed.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be understood as a carefully bounded morning transition, using words and water to recognize that one part of the day has ended and another has begun. It remains uncertain whether the tablet preserves a complete explanation of the sequence or only its brief formulas. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What changes when you treat washing your hands at dawn as a deliberate boundary between the night that has ended and the day that is beginning?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the three recorded phrases quietly at first light and wash your hands once while noticing the transition into morning. Do not treat this as a required ritual or prescription.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 152'-156'

title: Don't Fear, Bastet
intro: This lesson examines a healing spell from the Metternich Stela involving Bastet, a cat, and poison. It is presented as a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not as a modern prescription.
body:
The Metternich Stela records this as the third cat spell, in a section identified as another spell like it. The source is the Metternich Stela, section E, from the 30th Dynasty in the 4th century BC. The spell addresses Bastet before addressing poison affecting a suffering cat.

In the text's own terms, the speaker first reassures the goddess by reciting, "Don't fear, don't fear, Bastet." The speaker then asserts that Bastet has control over all the gods and commands, "Come out after my speech, you bad poison that is in any limb of the cat who is suffering!" The logic joins reassurance, divine authority, and a direct command for the poison to leave.

What is documented ends there: the record preserves the words and their stated purpose, but it does not explain the cat's condition or the outcome. Read now, this passage can be studied as an example of how speech, divine power, and healing were connected in the text. Whether the spell was understood as symbolic, ritual, or practically effective remains uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: What changes when a healing command begins by reassuring the deity whose authority is being invoked?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded phrases aloud once, then write a short note about how reassurance and command are arranged in the spell. This is not a reconstruction of the rite and should not be used to treat poison or illness.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Poison and animal illness require qualified modern veterinary care; do not use this text as a treatment for a cat or any other animal.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section E, Another spell like it

title: Drive Away the Lions of Meru
intro: This lesson examines a travel-protection charm from the Harris Magical Papyrus. It names lions, crocodiles, and poisonous reptiles as dangers from which the owner sought protection.
body:
The Harris Magical Papyrus, also cited as BM EA 10042, preserves a charm from the 19th-20th Dynasty, around 1200-1100 BC. The charm was carried by its owner while travelling and was intended to guard against predators of land and river. Its source citation identifies it as a charm against sea and river monsters.

In its own terms, the charm addresses the lord of the gods directly: "Hail, lord of the gods! Drive away from me the lions of the country of Meru, and the crocodiles which come forth from the river, and the bite of all poisonous reptiles." The logic is direct naming and removal: dangerous animals and their bites are identified, then commanded to stay away from the traveller.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this charm can be understood as a focused expression of vulnerability during travel and a wish to make dangerous surroundings safer. It also shows how protection could be carried with the person rather than fixed to a place. The record does not explain how often it was recited, what physical form the charm took, or whether its users regarded it as guaranteed protection.
reflection: When travelling through places that feel dangerous or unfamiliar, what specific fears would you want to name before choosing practical ways to stay safe?
practice: As a modern practice, write a brief travel safety reminder that names the risks you expect to encounter and the precautions you will take. Read it aloud before a journey; this is a present-day reflection exercise, not a reconstruction of the ancient rite.
safetyNote: The historical charm concerns lions, crocodiles, and poisonous reptiles. It is recorded for study and must not be treated as protection from wildlife or as a substitute for ordinary caution around animals.
sourceCitation: Harris Magical Papyrus (BM EA 10042) - Harris Magical Papyrus; Chabas, Le Papyrus Magique Harris (1860), charm against sea and river monsters

title: Invocation of Nusku, Protective Night Light
intro: This lesson examines a dawn invocation of Nusku in the Maqlu, an Akkadian and Standard Babylonian text from the first millennium BC. Nusku is presented as the protective night light whose work reaches its close at dawn.
body:
The third sequence of the Maqlu is associated with dawn. At first light, Nusku is invoked as the lamp that guarded the whole night and carried the working through the dark hours. The instruction then calls for an immediate greeting to the saviour and to the sun-god.

In its own terms, the sequence marks a transition. Nusku's protective light belongs to the night and has endured its dangers. Dawn becomes the hinge between those dangers and the day's deliverance, so the invocation closes the night work and turns toward the arriving day.

What is documented ends there: the record gives the timing, the identity of Nusku, the protective image of the lamp, and the order of the dawn greeting. Read now, this can be understood as a reflection on moving from danger into safety and from darkness into daylight. It remains uncertain how every ancient practitioner understood the saviour named in the sequence, because this record does not explain that figure further.
reflection: What part of your own night feels ready to be acknowledged as complete when the first light of day arrives?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, notice the first daylight you see and write one sentence about what you are leaving behind from the night and one sentence about what you are welcoming into the day.
safetyNote: The historical material uses the image of a lamp. No open flame is needed for this modern practice; use daylight or an ordinary electric light instead.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, third sequence (dawn)

title: Invocation of the Stars
intro: This lesson examines the opening movement of Maqlu, an Akkadian and Standard Babylonian anti-witchcraft text. It describes a nighttime address to the stars before the rest of the rite begins.
body:
Maqlu, meaning "Burning," opens after sunset with the sufferer facing the open sky. The opening section belongs to a work redacted in the late 2nd millennium BC and known from the 1st millennium BC. Its source context is the opening of Maqlu, as described in the cited overview.

In the ritual's own terms, the stars are named as the visible astral forms of the gods. The gods of the netherworld are asked to imprison the sorcerers and what has been sent against the sufferer. The gods of heaven are asked to purify the sufferer, while the whole cosmos is asked to pause and take the sufferer's side before any other rite begins.

What is documented ends there for this entry. Read now, this opening can be understood as a way of placing danger, cleansing, and protection within a cosmic setting before further ritual action. What remains uncertain is how the request for the cosmos to pause was understood or enacted, because the record gives no further detail here.
reflection: When you imagine the stars as the visible forms of divine powers, what kind of protection or cleansing would you ask the night sky to represent?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, look at the evening sky and write two brief sentences: one naming what you wish to set aside, and one describing what feeling clean or protected would mean to you. This is a personal reflection, not a reconstruction of the ancient rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu ("Burning"), opening section - Maqlu I, opening; Schwemer, CMAwRo overview

title: Isis, Isis, Come to Your Horus
intro: This lesson examines an Ancient Egyptian spell against a scorpion sting. It is recorded in section K of the Metternich Stela, from the 30th Dynasty, 4th century BC.
body:
The Metternich Stela records a summoning cry used when a scorpion has stung. In the spell, the call is made twice: Isis, Isis, come to your Horus! The sting is then reported as the gods report it, followed by a recitation of Isis's arrival.

In the spell's own terms, Isis comes with a mesh shirt on her chest and her arms spread. She offers reassurance, and the protection associated with her shelter extends from Horus to the person suffering. The sequence joins the divine summons, the description of the danger, and the arrival of protection.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this text can be studied as a focused expression of calling for divine aid and extending a protective image to someone in pain. The record does not establish how the spell was performed beyond its words, or how its users understood its practical effectiveness. Its historical setting is Ancient Egyptian, and its source is the Metternich Stela, held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
reflection: What does the movement from calling Isis for Horus to extending her shelter to the suffering person suggest to you about how protection was imagined in this spell?
practice: As a modern practice, read the recorded call quietly or write it in a journal, then note what kind of shelter or reassurance you would want during a frightening moment. This is a reflective exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Bites, stings, and infections are medical emergencies; seek treatment.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section K, Spell against a scorpion sting

title: Shamash Has Risen, I Reach
intro: This lesson presents a sunrise handwashing formula from the final tablet of the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It is spoken once the sun-god is visibly present and is followed by the next formula in the series.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records the words Shamash has risen, I reach as part of a sunrise handwashing action. The source citation places this passage at obv. 160'-161' of the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts within the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition. After this line, the series continues with When the witch crossed the river.

In its own terms, the formula joins visible sunrise, the presence of the sun-god, washing the hands, and a spoken sequence. The action appears at the close of the series, with the washing and words marking a transition into the following formula. The record describes the order of these actions but does not explain further what each phrase was believed to accomplish.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can be approached as a brief study of ritual timing, bodily cleansing, and the closing movement of a written sequence. What remains uncertain is the fuller meaning practitioners assigned to reaching toward Shamash and to the following river-crossing formula. The practice note identifies this as a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What changes in your understanding of this closing formula when you notice that its timing depends on the sun-god being visibly present?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, wash your hands at sunrise and read the two recorded phrases from the entry once. Then note what the sequence and the visible morning light bring to your attention.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 160'-161'

title: Sun, Come to Your Daughter
intro: This lesson examines the second of a set of cat spells from the Metternich Stela. It presents a chain of appeals to divine relatives for an injured animal suffering from bad poison.
body:
The Metternich Stela, a 30th Dynasty text from the 4th century BC, records this as another spell in its section E. The text gives the sequence: "Sun, come to your daughter! Shu, come to your wife! Isis, come to your sister!" It then asks them together to save her from the bad poison and to fell it.

The appeal works through kinship. Each deity is addressed by an exact relationship to the injured animal: daughter, wife, or sister. Calling the gods through these family ties presents the cat's danger as a matter requiring their attention, then joins their power in a request to overcome the poison.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can prompt reflection on how naming relationships gave urgency and structure to a healing appeal. The record does not explain the cat's condition, the meaning of "fell it" in practice, or whether the spell was accompanied by other actions, so those details remain uncertain.
reflection: What changes when a plea for healing is shaped through the precise family relationships among the beings being called upon?
practice: As a modern practice, read the recorded appeal once as a historical text, then write a short, non-magical statement about the kind of care and support an injured animal needs. Do not treat this as a medical remedy or reconstruction of the ancient rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Poisoning and animal illness require qualified veterinary care; do not use this text as a medical treatment.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section E, Another spell

title: Thoth's Protection at the Bed
intro: This lesson examines a bedside protection recitation from the Metternich Stela, an Ancient Egyptian source from the 30th Dynasty, 4th century BC. It presents Thoth and Isis as protective voices for Horus and for anyone who is suffering.
body:
