The finger gave the rite a physical model, while the tallow, wool, and recitation marked and prepared it in a prescribed sequence. The record presents this procedure as part of the Maqlu tradition, but does not explain the object's exact effect or identify a separate use for each material.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can be approached as an example of how a compact object and a spoken accusation were joined in an ancient ritual setting. The surviving description leaves uncertain how practitioners understood the finger's precise role, and that meaning remains debated or unavailable from this record alone. Its value for study lies in the careful sequence preserved by the text.
reflection: What might the combination of a finger-shaped object and the phrase "My murderess, my witch, and my sorceress" suggest about how the ritual gave form to its concern?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded incantation once and journal about how the clay finger, tallow, and red wool shape your understanding of the ritual sequence. Do not treat this reading exercise as a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and need not be attempted. A reader can engage with the description without handling tallow or recreating the wrapped clay object.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 66'

title: The Reed Cross
intro: This lesson examines the Reed Cross, a constructed object recorded in the fourth tablet of the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The entry describes its materials, arrangement, and accompanying words.
body:
The source records two full reeds laid across one another and tied at their intersection with black string. Tallow figurines were set inverted at the four ends. The cross was rubbed with tallow and wrapped in red wool while the words Burn, burn were recited. This passage is cited from Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 60'-64', in 7th century BC manuscripts of the Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition.

In the procedure's own terms, the crossed reeds created a single constructed form, while the black string fixed the intersection. The inverted figurines, tallow covering, red wool, and repeated words gave the object a prescribed arrangement and action. The record documents these elements, but does not explain the separate meaning assigned to each material.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can be approached as a study of how a ritual object was assembled through crossing, binding, covering, and spoken repetition. The exact purpose of the Reed Cross within the larger ritual, and the intended significance of its colors and figurines, remains uncertain from this entry alone. It should therefore be treated as a historical reconstruction for study, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What might the sequence of crossing, binding, covering, and reciting Burn, burn suggest about how this object was meant to be understood, while remembering that its exact purpose remains uncertain?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, arrange two pencils in a cross and tie them together with ordinary string. Write a short note describing which parts of the historical record are documented and which meanings remain unknown.
safetyNote: The historical procedure includes tallow figurines and should be treated as material for study only. Do not attempt to reproduce the historical rite or handle animal-derived materials for this purpose.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 60'-64'

title: The Witch Who Roams the Streets
intro: This lesson examines a figurine rite from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet involving a witch imagined as wandering through the city. It focuses on the clay image, the materials placed within it, and the spoken phrase associated with the finished figure.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records the making of a clay figurine of the witch described as one who roams the streets. Tallow was set in the epigastrium, and cornel wood was driven into the kidneys. The phrase The witch, she who roams the streets was recited over the completed image. This passage appears in the obv. 42'-43' section of Tablet III, in 7th century BC manuscripts.

In its own terms, the rite joined a physical image to a named witch figure. The clay body provided a form for the imagined witch, while the inserted materials marked particular areas of that body. The spoken phrase identified the figure and completed the action described in the record. The entry's tags identify this as a figurine and binding practice.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be studied as an example of how words, images, and inserted materials were combined in Mesopotamian ritual thought. It remains uncertain what exact effect the practitioners expected from the tallow, the cornel wood, or the completed figurine, because this record does not explain their individual meanings.
reflection: What do the figurine's marked body areas make you wonder about the relationship between physical representation and ritual control in this passage?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded phrase once and write a few sentences about how the clay figure and its inserted materials shape your understanding of the rite. Do not try to reconstruct the historical procedure.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. It includes tallow and the insertion of material into a figurine, so keep modern study limited to reading and reflection.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 42'-43' (Tablet III section)

title: Three Knots of White Wool
intro: This lesson examines a knot rite from the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It joins three knots in white wool with an incantation, followed by undoing the knots and casting the band into a crucible.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records three knots tied in a band of white wool while the phrase Of the Sun, who is his father, who is his mother? is recited. The knots are then undone, and the wool band is cast into the crucible. The source is cited at Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 67', in 7th century BC manuscripts from the Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition.

In its own terms, the rite joined spoken words with a physical sequence. Tying made three knots, while undoing them enacted their removal. The final casting of the band into the crucible completed the movement away from the knotted form. The record describes this sequence but does not explain every detail of its symbolism.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be considered a compact study in how binding and release were represented through wool, knots, speech, and deliberate undoing. It may invite reflection on the usefulness of completing a process by reversing its first action. The exact meaning of the solar incantation and the reason for the number three remain uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: What might change in your understanding of release when you picture it not as a single act, but as the careful undoing of three separate knots?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, not a reconstruction of the ancient rite, tie three loose knots in a piece of yarn, read the recorded phrase, then undo the knots and write about one process you are ready to complete or set aside. Do not use a crucible, heat, or flame.
safetyNote: The historical procedure ends with casting the wool band into a crucible. For safety, do not reproduce that step with heat or flame; this entry is for study rather than practical reenactment.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 67'

title: Three Sticks of Cornel
intro: This lesson examines a counter-rite in the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The recorded procedure uses three cornel sticks, tallow, red wool, and a spoken reference to zikurrudu, described as "cutting of the throat" witchcraft.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records three cornel sticks rubbed with tallow and wrapped with red wool. While performing this action, the practitioner recited, "Whoever you are, O witch, who performs zikurrudu-magic against me." The source citation places this passage at obv. 65', and the surviving manuscripts belong to the 7th century BC.

In its own terms, this was a counter-rite directed against a witch and the named form of witchcraft. The physical preparation of the sticks was joined to spoken identification of the threat. The rite therefore worked through both the prepared objects and the words that opposed the harmful magic described in the incantation.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the passage can be studied as a compact example of how a protective response joined materials, wrapping, and speech. It remains uncertain how the cornel, tallow, and red wool were understood beyond the actions recorded here, or how the rite was carried out in its wider setting. This entry does not establish a modern use for the procedure.
reflection: What changes in your reading when the three prepared sticks are considered together with the direct naming of the witch and zikurrudu?
practice: As a modern study practice, copy the recorded procedure into a journal and separate the material actions from the spoken words. This is a reading exercise, not a reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and should not be attempted. Do not handle the historical materials as part of a reconstruction.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 65'

title: Two Cornel Sticks at the Outer Gate
intro: This lesson examines a doorway rite from the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It uses two cornel sticks, charged by recitation and placed at the two sides of an outer gate.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records this rite at obv. 119'-121'. In manuscripts from the 7th century BC, the procedure calls for an incantation to be recited over two sticks of cornel. One stick is then set to the right and the other to the left of the outer gate. The text describes the witch involved as constantly roaming over all lands.

In its own terms, the rite joins spoken charging with threshold placement. The recitation gives the sticks their ritual role, while positioning one on each side creates a guarded pair at the entrance. The outer gate is therefore treated as the point where protection is established and watched from both sides.

What is documented ends there: the record gives the materials, recitation, placement, and protective setting, but not the full incantation or a further explanation of how the rite was expected to operate. Read now, this entry can prompt reflection on how boundaries are marked with words and objects. It remains uncertain how different practitioners understood the sticks or how consistently this procedure was performed.
reflection: What does placing two charged objects on opposite sides of an outer gate suggest about the way this rite imagined protection at a boundary?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, arrange two ordinary, non-ritual objects on opposite sides of a doorway as a visual reminder of a personal boundary. You may read a short statement about what you want the threshold to represent.
safetyNote: Cornel is a plant material, and the historical procedure is recorded for study rather than as a modern prescription. Do not treat this entry as instructions for sourcing or using cornel.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 119'-121'

title: Washing Over Her Likeness in Flour
intro: This lesson examines a handwashing rite recorded in the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It uses a likeness drawn in flour and a clay figurine as part of an anti-witchcraft act.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a rite in which the witch's likeness was drawn in flour inside a washbasin. A clay figurine representing her was placed on the flour image, and the patient washed his hands over both while reciting. The instruction then says to return into the house. The passage comes from the Mesopotamian, or Akkadian and Standard Babylonian, tradition and survives in 7th century BC manuscripts, at obv. 140'-142'.

In the rite's own terms, the image and figurine provided a material focus for the act. Washing the patient's hands over the representation connected the person's cleansing with the likeness placed beneath it. The recitation formed part of the procedure, while the return into the house marked its completion. The record does not explain the words of the recitation or describe any further treatment of the image or figurine.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can prompt reflection on how a person's likeness might be used to represent a threat and to frame a return to safety. It should remain a historical study rather than a modern prescription. The exact purpose of every action and the wording of the recitation remain uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: What might the placement of a likeness beneath washing hands have communicated about removing danger and re-entering the home?
practice: As a modern study practice, read this entry aloud and write a short note about how the flour likeness, clay figurine, handwashing, and return into the house work together in the recorded sequence. Do not treat this as a reconstruction of the rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 140'-142'

title: Chaff, Wall-Plaster and Soot
intro: This lesson examines a fumigant recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It combines chaff, wall-plaster and soot with the repeated cry "kukru, kukru, kukru" and involves burning the mixture.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a fumigant made by combining chaff, wall-plaster and soot. The mixture was burned while the incantation was recited, including the tripled cry "kukru, kukru, kukru". The source is Mesopotamian, in Akkadian or Standard Babylonian, and is preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts. The citation identifies this passage as obv. 98'.

In its own terms, the procedure joined agricultural waste with materials scraped from the house and transformed them through fire and smoke. The recited words accompanied the fumigation, making the spoken cry part of the procedure rather than a separate statement. The record describes the action, but does not explain the specific effect assigned to each ingredient or to the repeated cry.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can prompt reflection on how ordinary remnants of field and house were brought together in a formal act. It also shows how material action and spoken repetition could be presented as one unit. It remains uncertain what precise purpose the fumigant served and how practitioners understood the individual materials.
reflection: What might the combination of chaff, wall-plaster and soot suggest to you about the relationship between agricultural work, household space and ritual action?
practice: As a modern practice, read the entry slowly and journal about what changes when ordinary household materials are treated as meaningful symbols. Do not burn or combine the historical ingredients.
safetyNote: The historical fumigation is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Burning plant material, plaster or soot can create a fire hazard and harmful smoke, especially indoors.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 98'

title: Handwash Water of Eight Materials
intro: This lesson examines the prepared water used for the final washings in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The water was steeped with eight named materials, and the hands were washed in it while reciting Until you rise.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records water prepared with tamarisk, soapwort, a date pit, chaff, gypsum, a ring of shubu stone, kukru, and juniper. After these materials were steeped in the water, the hands were washed in it during the final washings. The source is represented in 7th century BC manuscripts, and the cited passage is Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 157'-159'.

In the procedure's own terms, the prepared water and the washing belong together. The many materials were combined in water, and the spoken phrase Until you rise accompanied the handwashing. The record presents this as a defined closing action rather than as an ordinary washing with plain water.

Read now, this entry can invite attention to how a ritual gives a final washing a carefully prepared setting. What remains uncertain is why each material was selected and what meaning practitioners assigned to the phrase. This account is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What might the transition from a specially prepared washing to the words Until you rise suggest to you about the role of endings in a ritual?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the phrase Until you rise once and write a short note about what you want to leave behind or rise from today. Do not prepare the historical wash.
safetyNote: The historical material includes named plants and other substances, so it should be treated as a study record rather than a practical recipe. Do not prepare or use this mixture, ingest any ingredient, or use the named plants medicinally.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 157'-159'

title: Inventory for the Burning Rite
intro: This lesson examines a late Babylonian material list associated with the Maqlu anti-witchcraft ritual. It records objects prepared before a burning ceremony, but does not provide instructions for using them.
body:
The source is Mesopotamian, in Akkadian or Standard Babylonian, and belongs to late Babylonian ritual material from the 5th century BC. The list names two holy water vessels, two small bowls, two hand towels, an erimmu-fruit of the mountain, an iron cross, a lamp, and figurines made from tamarisk wood, cedar wood, bronze, and wax. It also includes bitumen, sesame pomace, a mountain stone, and a hand of tamarisk.

The entry is an inventory rather than a description of actions. It shows that the ceremony involved several kinds of vessels, cloths, light, natural materials, and figurines made from different substances. The record does not state how these objects were arranged, what was burned, or what each material represented in the rite's own terms.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this list can be approached as evidence of careful preparation and material variety within an anti-witchcraft ceremony, without turning it into a modern recipe. It remains uncertain how each item was used or understood, because this entry records materials rather than instructions.
reflection: What might you learn by paying attention to the different materials named in this inventory without assuming what any of them meant?
practice: As a modern study practice, copy the inventory into a journal and divide it into categories such as vessels, textiles, light, figurines, and other materials. This is an exercise in reading the historical record, not a reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical list includes a lamp and combustible materials, but it is recorded here for study and must not be attempted. Do not burn or recreate the listed materials.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, late Babylonian ritual material list - Abusch & Schwemer, The Anti-Witchcraft Ritual Maqlu (5th-century BC family archive material list)

title: Juniper and Kukru
intro: This lesson examines a fumigant recorded at the opening of the sixth tablet of the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It uses juniper and kukru, together with the self-identification "Enlil is my head, my face is umu."
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records juniper and kukru being burned together on a censer as the opening fumigant of the sixth tablet. The accompanying self-identification is "Enlil is my head, my face is umu." The source is part of the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition, preserved in seventh-century BC manuscripts, with this passage cited at obv. 96'.

In the procedure as recorded, the fumigant and spoken incantation belong together. The plant materials are placed on the censer and burned while the incantation is recited, making the scent-producing action and the verbal declaration one opening act. The record does not explain the separate meanings of juniper, kukru, or the phrase.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can invite attention to how materials and self-identification were joined at the start of a ritual, without claiming that the modern reader can recover every intended meaning. It remains uncertain or debated what kukru was, and what precise role the self-identification served within the tablet.
reflection: What changes when the fumigant and the words "Enlil is my head, my face is umu" are considered as one opening gesture rather than as separate parts?
practice: As a modern practice, write the recorded self-identification in a journal and read it aloud once as an exercise in noticing how a formal statement shapes attention. This is a reflective exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Burning juniper and kukru indoors creates fire and inhalation risks.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 96'

title: Kukru and Soapwort
intro: This lesson examines a two-ingredient fumigant recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It pairs kukru and soapwort with the incantation "My sorceress is a qumqummatu".
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records burning kukru with soapwort while reciting the incantation "My sorceress is a qumqummatu". This entry belongs to a long run of kukru-based smokes in the text. The source is associated with Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition, with manuscripts dating to the 7th century BC.

In the recorded procedure, the plant materials were burned together as a fumigant, and spoken words accompanied the smoke. The entry gives the ingredients, the action, and the incantation, but does not explain further how the materials or words were understood to work.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can draw attention to the close pairing of physical smoke and spoken language in the ritual record, without treating the procedure as a modern recipe. It remains uncertain what kukru specifically referred to in this context and how practitioners interpreted the phrase beyond its place in the rite.
reflection: What do you notice about the way the recorded smoke and the spoken phrase are presented as one ritual action?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the recorded incantation once and write a few sentences about how its wording changes your sense of the fumigant. Do not burn or handle the listed plants.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves fire, smoke, and plant material, creating fire and inhalation risks. It is recorded for study and should not be attempted.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 97'

title: Parched Roasted Flour
intro: This lesson examines parched roasted flour in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The material appears in two consecutive rites and is later poured out repeatedly and used to draw around entrances.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records parched roasted flour at obv. 78'-80' and 90'-93'. The flour is used with two incantations in sequence. One incantation includes the parenthetical note "for fifteen days," while another contains the line "Splendid is my appearance, splendid is my countenance." The same material is later poured out repeatedly and used to draw around the entrances.

In the text's own terms, the material links spoken words with repeated physical actions. Its use around entrances gives the flour a boundary-making role, while the repeated pouring and the stated duration connect the rite to continuity over time. The confident language about appearance and countenance adds a concern with how the practitioner is presented or perceived within the sequence.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can be approached as a study of repeated action, spoken confidence, and the marking of thresholds. It remains uncertain how every step was understood by the original practitioners or how the two incantations related to one another beyond their sequence. The record supports description of the actions, but not a complete reconstruction of their intended effect.
reflection: What might the repeated use of one dry material, first with words and later at entrances, suggest about the relationship between personal presence and protected boundaries in this rite?
practice: As a modern reflective practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the recorded phrase aloud and write briefly about what qualities you want to bring to your own presence and boundaries. Do not use flour or attempt the historical procedure.
safetyNote: This is a historical preparation described for study, not a modern recipe. Do not prepare, ingest or apply it; treat every listed material as unverified and not food-safe.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 78'-80', 90'-93'

title: Pure Oil, Clear Oil
intro: This lesson examines a measured oil anointing recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The procedure uses one tenth of a litre of oil across three consecutive incantations, ending with anointing the patient's entire body.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a procedure using one tenth of a litre of oil. Three incantations accompany the preparation and use of the oil: "I am impregnating you, my self," "Pure oil, clear oil," and "Enlil is my head, Sirius is my form." The final words are spoken while the patient's entire body is anointed.

Within the procedure's own terms, measurement, spoken formula, and bodily application belong together. The oil is first addressed through the incantations, then used in a complete anointing. The words connect the patient with purity, clarity, Enlil, and Sirius, although the record does not explain these connections further.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be understood as a carefully sequenced act in which quantity, repeated speech, and full-body treatment create a unified ritual. The exact intended effect of each phrase, and how practitioners understood the relationship between the oil, Enlil, and Sirius, remains uncertain from this entry alone. It is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What might the careful measure of the oil and the progression from spoken preparation to whole-body anointing suggest about how ritual order shaped the experience of care?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the three recorded phrases silently and journal about how their sequence changes your sense of the oil, the body, and the final anointing. Do not apply oil to another person.
safetyNote: This is a historical preparation described for study, not a modern recipe. Do not prepare, ingest or apply it; treat every listed material as unverified and not food-safe.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 130'-133'

title: The Divination Oil of Seven
intro: This lesson examines a vessel-divination preparation recorded in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The procedure uses clear Oasis oil, repeated groups of seven, and a boy who gazes into the oil.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden records this preparation in P. London-Leiden, col. III, 5-19 (Griffith & Thompson). In the text, seven new bricks are used before they have been turned over: three tiles go beneath the oil and four around the child. Seven clean loaves and seven lumps of salt are also arranged around a new dish.

The dish is filled gradually with clean Oasis oil so that the oil remains perfectly clear. A pure boy, clothed in clean linen, gazes into the surface while the invocation is recited seven times. The repeated number seven organizes the bricks, loaves, salt, and spoken invocation, while the clear oil provides the surface for the act of viewing.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be studied as a carefully ordered vessel-divination scene in which materials, purity, arrangement, and repetition define the procedure. The record does not explain what the boy was expected to see, how the vision was interpreted, or whether the rite was considered successful. Those points remain uncertain from this entry alone.
reflection: What might the repeated use of seven, the clear oil, and the carefully arranged objects have communicated to someone participating in this divination?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry slowly and journal what details make the procedure feel ordered or focused. Do not treat this as a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves a boy, but it is recorded here for study and must not be attempted with children. Use reading and journaling instead of trying to recreate the rite.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. III, 5-19 (Griffith & Thompson)

title: The Sea-Karab Stone
intro: This lesson examines a short fumigant instruction from the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. It names the sea-karab stone as a means of bringing a person who died by drowning into a vessel.
body:
The source is the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden, from Graeco-Roman Egypt in the 3rd century AD. In column III, lines 26-27, it records the instruction to put the sea-karab stone on a brazier to bring in one who died by drowning. The description identifies this as one of several recipes keyed to specific categories of the dead.

In its own terms, the procedure depends on a direct correspondence between the named stone and the manner of death. The stone is placed on the brazier as a fumigant, and the intended result is the arrival of the drowned person in the vessel. The category of the dead determines which recipe is used.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry shows a tightly focused link between a material name, a manner of death, and a summoning result. The record does not explain what the stone was, what the vessel contained, or how practitioners understood the arrival. Whether the instruction was intended as a literal working, a symbolic formula, or part of a larger ritual remains uncertain.
reflection: What does the close matching of the sea-karab stone to a drowned person suggest about how the practitioners organized different kinds of the dead in their ritual language?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the instruction once and journal about the three linked elements: the stone, the manner of death, and the vessel. This is a reflective exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical instruction involves placing a material on a brazier, with possible flame and smoke. Do not burn or heat materials as a modern reconstruction; study the text without attempting the procedure.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. III, 26-27

title: The Seven Planetary Perfumes
intro: This lesson examines a late antique correspondence table from the Graeco-Roman Egyptian Leiden Papyrus W. It pairs seven aromatics and seven flowers with the seven classical planets.
body:
The papyrus, dated to about the 3rd century AD, records a sequence of planetary perfumes. It assigns styrax to Saturn, malabathrum to Jupiter, costus to Mars, frankincense to the Sun, nard to Venus, cassia to Hermes, and myrrh to the Moon. The same text also lists seven flowers: nard, marjoram, lily, lotus, buttercup, narcissus, and white violet.

In its own terms, the table worked through correspondence. Each classical planet was linked with a particular aromatic, creating a structured set of seven planetary associations. The flowers formed a second matching group, although this record does not specify which individual flower belonged to which planet. The source presents these pairings as a table of relationships rather than as a modern prescription.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the list can be studied as an example of how planetary symbolism organized scents and flowers into ordered groups. It may invite reflection on how classification gives ritual materials meaning, but the record does not explain how the perfumes were used or what results were expected. It remains uncertain whether the flowers had fixed individual planetary assignments in the papyrus or were simply presented as a related set.
reflection: What might you notice about the difference between the clearly assigned perfumes and the flowers whose individual planetary pairings are not given?
practice: As a modern study practice, copy the seven planetary perfume assignments into a journal and make a separate list of the seven flowers without assigning them to planets. Note which details are documented and which would require speculation.
safetyNote: The historical material names aromatic plants and flowers. Study the list without burning, ingesting, or using any named plant medicinally; this is not a modern prescription.
sourceCitation: Leiden Papyrus W - P. Leiden W, seven perfumes and seven flowers

title: Thyme and Sesame
intro: This lesson examines a fumigant rite from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, a Mesopotamian work preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts. It records thyme and sesame burned against sorcery, followed immediately by a separate burning of chaff.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet, in obv. 71'-72', records the first fumigant of the fifth tablet. Thyme and sesame were burned while an incantation was recited against "my sorceress and the woman who instigates sorcery against me." The next rite burned chaff alone, with the words "Who has twined chaff together."

In the recorded procedure, spoken incantation and the burning of plant material formed a sequence. The first fumigation addressed the alleged sorceress and the woman said to be instigating sorcery. The immediate chaff rite followed as its own action, with a separate spoken phrase. The record presents these actions in ritual order, but does not explain the substances beyond their use in fumigation.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can be approached as evidence of how a Mesopotamian ritual connected smoke, recited words, and a response to perceived sorcery. The precise intended meaning of the thyme, sesame, and chaff, and how practitioners understood their differing roles, remains uncertain from this record alone. This study is not a reconstruction of the rite.
reflection: What might the strict sequence of thyme and sesame followed by chaff suggest to you about how the ritual organized a response to perceived sorcery?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry aloud without performing the rite, then journal the two-stage sequence and note which details are directly documented and which remain uncertain.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves fire, smoke, and burned plant material, creating fire and inhalation risks. Do not burn the materials or attempt the historical fumigation; study it only through reading and reflection.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 71'-72'

title: Categories of the Dead
intro: This lesson examines a functional classification of the dead in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. It focuses on how different conditions of death were linked with different methods of summoning into a vessel.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden records several operational categories: a spirit, a drowned man, a murdered man, a damned spirit, and a living man who can also be summoned into the vessel. Each category is associated with its own fumigant. The material appears in P. London-Leiden, col. III, 24-28 and col. VI, 1-10, from Graeco-Roman Egypt in the 3rd century AD.

In the handbook's own terms, classification determined method. The way a person died was treated as relevant to how that person could be reached, and the fumigant changed according to the category. The inclusion of a living man shows that the vessel was not limited only to the dead.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry presents a practical taxonomy rather than a single general idea of the dead. It suggests that practitioners understood access as dependent on a person's condition and manner of death. What remains uncertain is how these categories were understood in every case and how the procedures were actually carried out.
reflection: What might the inclusion of a living man among these categories suggest about the boundaries between the dead, the living, and the vessel in this handbook?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry and make a simple table with the five categories named in the record. Beside each one, note that the method was said to change according to the category, without attempting to reconstruct the rite.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. III, 24-28; col. VI, 1-10

title: From Petition to Compulsion
intro: This lesson examines an escalation sequence in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The text moves from inviting a god to appear in a lamp ritual toward a spoken compulsion.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden records this sequence in P. London-Leiden, col. VI, 21-27 and col. VIII, 1-11. If the god does not appear, the operator recites a compulsion that identifies himself with Abydos, Osiris and Anubis, and declares, "I am the Ram's face, Youth is my name."

In the text's own terms, the procedure escalates in stages. The operator first invites the entity, then presents himself as joined to greater powers, and finally withholds what the entity wants. The sequence is explicit in the text rather than improvised, making the change from petition to compulsion part of the method.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the passage offers a focused example of how authority is constructed through ritual speech and identification. The record does not explain whether the appearance was understood as literal, visionary, symbolic, or debated by different readers, so that point remains uncertain. Its value for study lies in tracing the prescribed escalation without treating it as a modern instruction.
reflection: What changes in the operator's relationship with the summoned god when an invitation becomes a claim of identity and then a compulsion?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the record's escalation in silence and write three neutral labels in a journal: invite, identify, withhold. Note what each stage adds to the structure without attempting to reconstruct the lamp ritual.
safetyNote: The historical material involves a lamp, so do not use flame or attempt to reconstruct the rite. This entry is for reading and study rather than modern ritual practice.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. VI, 21-27; col. VIII, 1-11

title: Hazardous and Protected Materials
intro: This lesson examines hazardous materials named in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet and the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The lists include substances now recognized as poisonous, controlled, or associated with protected species.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet and the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden record ingredient lists that include sulphur, copper sulphate, alum, opium, mandrake, henbane, hoopoe, hawk, crocodile, and shrew. The cited passages belong to the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 105'-110', and P. London-Leiden, col. III, 24 and col. XXIV, 1-14. The traditions represented are Mesopotamian and Graeco-Roman Egyptian.

In these records, the substances appear as materials called for by the handbooks. The record does not provide a modern safety assessment or establish a single purpose or mechanism for every listed item. What it does make clear is that an ingredient list from these texts cannot be treated as an ordinary recipe.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this material is best approached as evidence of historical practice and as a warning about the distance between ancient instructions and present law and medicine. Several preparations are acutely toxic, some materials are controlled substances, and several named animals are protected species. The exact intended use and reasoning for every item remain uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: How does recognizing the legal and medical danger of these materials change the way you read an ancient magical handbook as a historical document?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded ingredient list without collecting or handling any of its materials, then write a short note identifying which items the record describes as poisonous, controlled, or associated with protected species. This is not a reconstruction of the historical procedure.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Do not obtain, ingest, prepare, burn, or handle these substances or animal materials; some are toxic or controlled, and several animals are protected species.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet; Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 105'-110'; P. London-Leiden, col. III, 24; col. XXIV, 1-14

title: Named Kinds of Witchcraft
intro: This lesson examines how the Mesopotamian Maqlu texts classified different forms of witchcraft. The central task was to identify the kind of attack before selecting a response.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records several named forms of attack, including zikurrudu magic, hate-magic, and the sending of spittle. Elsewhere, Maqlu identifies a manifestation as "the grip of the mountain, be it the epilepsy, the offspring of Shulpaea". These references appear in 7th century BC manuscripts of the Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition.

In its own terms, the system depended on matching a diagnosis to a specific counter-rite and its associated material. The practitioner therefore began with classification rather than treatment. Naming the type of magic was not merely descriptive; it determined which response was considered appropriate.

What is documented ends there: the record shows the categories and the importance of matching rite to diagnosis, but it does not provide enough information here to reconstruct each response. Read now, this lesson highlights a method of careful distinction before action. It remains uncertain how every named category was understood in practice or how consistently these classifications were applied. The historical mention of epilepsy should not be treated as a modern diagnosis or medical explanation.
reflection: How might distinguishing between different kinds of harm change the way you interpret a problem before deciding how to respond?
practice: As a modern study practice, make a two-column note with the named categories in this entry on one side and the kinds of responses the text says they required on the other. Keep the second column limited to what the record actually states, and mark unknown details as uncertain.
safetyNote: The reference to epilepsy is historical and should not be used for diagnosis or treatment. This entry is for study and does not provide a modern medical prescription.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet; Maqlu - Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 65', 77', 170'-174'; Maqlu, manifestations of witchcraft

title: The Harmful Spells This Database Omits
intro: This lesson concerns harmful recipes recorded in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The material includes procedures whose stated purposes were to blind, sedate, or kill a person, but those methods are deliberately not reproduced here.
body:
The London-Leiden handbook contains recipes for causing blindness, sedation, or death. The cited passages are recto column XIII, lines 11-26; column XXIII, lines 1-20; and column XXIV, lines 1-14. The source is associated with Graeco-Roman Egypt and dates to the 3rd century AD.

In their own terms, these procedures used substances or preparations intended to produce severe effects. The record mentions animal gall placed in food, drowned animals in wine, opium and scammony, and draughts made with mandrake and henbane. These details show that the texts present functional poisoning procedures rather than harmless symbolic actions.

What is documented ends there. The methods are omitted because several are dangerous and could cause serious harm or death. Read now, this entry supports historical study without turning harmful instructions into a usable recipe. Whether any particular procedure was effective in practice is not established by this entry, and the material should not be reconstructed or tested.
reflection: How should a study of the London-Leiden handbook preserve evidence of these harmful recipes while refusing to make their procedures usable today?
practice: As a modern practice, read this entry and write a short note distinguishing historical documentation from instructions for action. Do not attempt to recreate, test, or handle any of the substances or materials mentioned.
safetyNote: The historical procedures are recorded for study and must not be attempted. Several involve poisoning methods and potentially dangerous substances, including animal materials and named plants.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, recto col. XIII, 11-26; col. XXIII, 1-20; col. XXIV, 1-14

title: The Ritual Tablet as Choreography
intro: This lesson examines the ninth tablet of the Maqlu Ritual Tablet as a performance plan. Rather than serving as a simple reading list, it organizes actions, materials, gestures and incantations into a fixed sequence.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet survives in 7th century BC manuscripts in Akkadian, in the Standard Babylonian tradition. The ninth tablet records well over ninety distinct actions in performance order. It begins with treading on tamarisk and ends with sprinkling water toward sunrise. Each action is keyed to the opening line of an incantation found on tablets one through eight.

In its own terms, the tablet joined spoken text to precise movement and material handling. Its value lay in fixing when each action occurred, which material was used and which gesture accompanied the relevant incantation. The complete ritual was therefore structured as a timed sequence rather than approached as a collection of independent readings.

What is documented ends there: the record establishes order, materials, gestures and verbal cues, but it does not explain here what each action symbolized or how every performer understood it. Read now, this tablet can be studied as choreography, showing how ritual meaning was distributed across an entire night of coordinated acts. The exact experience of performing that sequence remains uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: How does reading the ninth tablet as choreography, rather than as a list of incantations, change your sense of where the ritual's meaning might have been located?
practice: As a modern study practice, make a simple timeline on paper with a beginning, several ordered steps and an ending. Use only the actions named in this record, and label the exercise as an analysis rather than a reconstruction of the rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 1-179' in full (Oracc CMAwRo Q002713)

title: What Ingredients Reveal About Access
intro: This lesson examines what a late Babylonian material list for the Maqlu burning rite can reveal about access, cost, and ritual supply networks. Its ingredients point to a full night-long ritual that required more than ordinary household materials.
body:
The list calls for two holy water vessels, a cross of iron, an erimmu-fruit of the mountain, a mountain stone, and figurines made from tamarisk, cedar, bronze, wax, bitumen, and sesame pomace. It is identified as late Babylonian Maqlu material from a 5th-century BC family archive list.

In its own terms, the rite depended on assembling several distinct materials and forms. Imported cedar, worked bronze, and iron point to a client with means and to a practitioner with supply lines. The range of substances suggests that carrying out the complete night-long ritual required organized access to goods, not merely knowledge of spoken words or gestures.

What is documented ends there: the list shows material requirements, but it does not state the price of each item, who personally paid, or how widely such a rite was available. Read now, this evidence makes ritual access an economic question as well as a religious one. The materials support the interpretation that some clients could commission a full rite because they had resources, while practitioners depended on networks that could obtain imported and worked goods. Exactly how common this level of access was remains uncertain.
reflection: What might the combination of imported, worked, and locally described materials suggest about the relationship between a client's resources and a practitioner's supply network?
practice: As a modern study practice, make a two-column note listing the materials in this record and what each one reveals about access or labor. Keep the exercise historical rather than trying to recreate the rite.
safetyNote: The historical material concerns a burning rite and is recorded for study only; do not attempt to recreate it or burn its ingredients.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, late Babylonian material list - Abusch & Schwemer, The Anti-Witchcraft Ritual Maqlu; 5th-century BC family archive list

title: What the Erotic Spells Actually Demanded
intro: This lesson examines erotic and relationship magic recorded in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The material comes from Graeco-Roman Egypt and includes potions, figures, rings, and amulets directed toward specific relationship outcomes.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden contains a large section on erotic compulsion. It records potions intended to make a named woman love or follow a man, a figure of Geb used to separate a couple, and rings and amulets meant to compel attendance. The texts also pair desire with language of wasting and fire.

In the texts' own terms, the target is specific rather than general. A potion, figure, ring, or amulet is treated as a means of directing an outcome toward a particular person or couple. The instructions describe action taken without the target's knowledge, making desire, separation, or attendance the result to be imposed.

Read now, this material is evidence about gender and power as well as ancient magical practice. One person's desire is given priority over another person's knowledge and choice, especially where a named woman is made to love or follow a man. It remains uncertain how often these procedures were performed or how successful they were. What is documented is the coercive ideal expressed by the texts, not proof that the desired outcome occurred.
reflection: What does the focus on a named target, hidden action, and compelled attendance reveal about the difference between desire and mutual consent?
practice: As a modern practice, write a short journal entry describing what mutual, informed, and freely given affection would look like in one relationship. Do not name or target another person in the exercise.
safetyNote: These historical coercive procedures are recorded for study and must not be attempted on any person. The lesson treats them as evidence about ancient practice, not as a technique for influencing someone without their knowledge.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, recto XII, XIII, XV, XXI, XXV; verso XIII, XIX, XXIX

title: Asafoetida at the Head of the Bed
intro: This lesson examines a night-protection rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It uses asafoetida, recitation, and a censer placed beside the sleeper's head.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a rite in which asafoetida is addressed with the words "Ha! my witch, my inseminatrix." The material is then placed on a censer at the head of the bed. The source is represented by 7th century BC manuscripts and belongs to the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition.

In its own terms, the rite joins spoken words with a pungent substance and its placement near the sleeping person. The record describes this as a night-protection practice, with the censer positioned beside the sleeper's head. Its documented action is therefore both recitation and fumigation in a private sleeping space.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can show how protection was connected to the bed, the vulnerable hours of night, and a strongly noticeable material. The record does not explain the phrase's meaning, the intended witch's identity, or the precise effect expected from the asafoetida. Those points remain uncertain from this entry alone.
reflection: What does the placement of the censer at the head of the bed suggest about how vulnerability during sleep was understood in this rite?
practice: As a modern study practice, copy the recorded instruction into a journal and note which details are directly documented: the phrase, the asafoetida, the censer, and the bed. This is a reflection exercise, not a reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Asafoetida fumes may pose an inhalation risk, and using a censer beside bedding creates a fire hazard.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 115'-116'

title: Be Off, Be Off
intro: This lesson examines a disposal rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. Its central actions involve roasted flour, burning remains, and carrying the materials away through an entrance or gate.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records an incantation followed by the repeated pouring out of roasted flour. After the burning, the remains were taken out through the entrance together with the crucible and thrown away. The record also gives a variant in which the brazier was carried out through the gate.

In the rite's own terms, removal was central to its action. The roasted flour was poured out repeatedly, and the remains of the burning were physically taken beyond the boundary of the entrance or gate. The disposal of the materials formed the closing movement described in this entry.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be understood as a structured act of ending, in which repeated pouring and removal marked the separation of the unwanted remains from the interior space. What the incantation said, what the roasted flour represented, and why the two disposal methods were both included remain uncertain from this record alone. Its historical setting is the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition, preserved in seventh-century BC manuscripts.
reflection: What does the movement from repeated pouring to carrying the remains beyond the entrance suggest to you about how this rite marked an ending?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write one sentence naming something you are ready to set aside. Read it aloud, then place the paper in ordinary recycling without burning it.
safetyNote: This historical fire rite involved hot residues. It is recorded for study and must not be attempted; do not handle burning materials, hot ashes, crucibles, or braziers.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 90'-91'

title: Be Spewed Out, You Poison
intro: This lesson examines an ancient Egyptian spell against poison from the Metternich Stela. It treats venom as a hostile force that can be commanded out while Horus restores the patient to life.
body:
The spell is recorded in section D of the Metternich Stela, an ancient Egyptian source from the 30th Dynasty, dated to the 4th century BC. The source is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art as 50.85 and identifies this passage as a spell against poison.

In its own terms, the spell addresses venom as though it were a hostile person. It commands, "Be spewed out, you poison! Come, come out on the ground!" The poison is then described as enchanted, constrained, spat upon, trampled, weakened, blinded, reversed, and finally lost, all through the authority of Horus. The patient is raised at the close with the words, "Stand up, you who are in sadness, for Horus has endowed you with life!"

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage shows healing language built around confrontation, reversal, and the restoration of strength. It may invite reflection on how naming an illness as an opponent can give structure to fear. The record does not tell us whether the spell was understood as a complete treatment, a spoken accompaniment to other care, or both, so its practical use remains uncertain.
reflection: What changes when poison is imagined not as an invisible substance, but as an opponent that can be ordered to leave?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write a short, non-medical statement about something you want to release from your thoughts, then read it aloud and set the page aside. Do not use this exercise in place of medical care.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Snakebite and scorpion envenomation are medical emergencies; seek professional treatment immediately.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section D, Spell against poison

title: Burning the Shurpu at the River
intro: This lesson examines the morning disposal of the ritual fire described in the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The recorded action is to carry the shurpu-fire out through the entrance or take it to the river and throw it away.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a morning fire-disposal rite. In the cited passage, the fire is taken out through the entrance, or carried all the way to the river, where it is thrown away. The source is associated with Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition, with manuscripts dating to the 7th century BC.

In its recorded terms, the rite ends by removing the ritual fire from the place where the work occurred. The two routes given are the entrance or the river, and both lead away from the ritual setting. The act described is therefore a deliberate disposal rather than the continued keeping of the fire.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be considered a study of how a ritual conclusion was expressed through carrying something away and discarding it. The record does not explain the full symbolism of the entrance, the river, or the fire, so their precise meanings remain uncertain. Any broader interpretation should remain separate from what the passage directly records.
reflection: What might change in your understanding of release when you distinguish between setting something aside and deliberately carrying it away?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, write one short sentence naming something you are ready to set down, then read the sentence aloud and place the paper in a safe recycling or storage place. This is a modern exercise in reflection, not a reconstruction of the historical fire rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves transporting burning material and is recorded here for study only; it must not be attempted. Do not carry or dispose of burning material, especially near entrances, waterways, people, or buildings.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 138'-139'

title: Evil Udug-Demon to Your Steppe
intro: This lesson examines a perimeter rite from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It concerns an udug-demon, an outer entrance, and a boundary drawn with roasted flour after the burning is removed.
body:
The record comes from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, in the Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition. The surviving manuscripts date to the 7th century BC, and the source citation places this passage at obv. 92'-93'. It describes a rite performed at the outer entrance, naming the udug-demon and drawing around the entrances with roasted flour.

In the terms recorded here, the rite establishes a boundary after the burning is removed. The incantation is directed toward the outer entrance, while the flour is used to mark the entrances. The action joins spoken naming with a visible perimeter, fixing the boundary around the doorway.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can be understood as a study of how a doorway was made the focus of protective boundary work in the text. It does not explain the full meaning of the udug-demon, the exact form of the incantation, or how practitioners understood every step. Those details remain uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: What might the contrast between naming the udug-demon and marking the entrance with flour suggest about the relationship between words and boundaries in this rite?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, sketch an outer doorway and mark a simple boundary around it on paper. Write a few words about what a boundary means to you; this is not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical description refers to burning and is recorded for study. Do not attempt to recreate the burning or the historical procedure.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 92'-93'

title: Holding the Scorpion's Mouth Shut
intro: This lesson examines an Ancient Egyptian confrontation spell associated with a scorpion or its image. It appears in Papyrus Turin 1993 and commands the threatening force to remain still.
body:
The text comes from the Ancient Egyptian tradition of the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC. It is recorded as Borghouts spell 105 in P. Turin 1993, verso 1, 1-8, with a related reference to spell 106. The entry describes a recitation made over a scorpion or its representation.

In its own terms, the spell works through direct command and threat. The speaker declares that the scorpion's mouth will be closed and threatens to cut off the seventy-seven heads, the hand of Horus, and the eye of Seth if the scorpion does not keep still. Its logic is confrontation: naming consequences is meant to force silence and prevent movement.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this spell shows how dangerous encounters could be addressed through authoritative speech and symbolic threats. It remains uncertain how the wording was used in particular situations or whether practitioners expected it to produce a physical effect. The historical record preserves the command, its imagery, and its source, but does not provide a modern medical procedure.
reflection: What does the spell's use of threats against the scorpion, Horus, and Seth suggest about how danger was imagined and controlled in this text?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry and source citation quietly, then journal about the difference between a historical command intended to control danger and a safe response to a real sting. Do not treat the exercise as a reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Never handle a live scorpion; envenomation is a medical emergency.
sourceCitation: Papyrus Turin 1993 - Borghouts spell 105 (P. Turin 1993, verso 1, 1-8); spell 106

title: I Am Raising the Torch
intro: This lesson examines a torch rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, a Mesopotamian text preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts. The rite invokes Grand Nusku, offspring of Anu, and combines figurines, aromatic materials, fire, and spoken words.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records fixing a tallow figurine and a wax figurine to a torch. Cedar, cypress, myrtle, ballukku-aromatic, and sweet reed are inserted into it, the prepared material is sprinkled over it, and the torch is kindled in burning sulphur. The recitation includes the phrase I am raising the torch. This passage is cited as obv. 27'-30'.

In its own terms, the rite joined shaped figures, fragrant substances, a torch, sulphur, and speech into one prepared action. The invocation of Grand Nusku, offspring of Anu, places the act within a sacred framework. The materials and flame appear to have been treated as parts of a unified ritual instrument, though the record does not explain each item's separate function.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage can be studied as an example of how material arrangement, fire, and recitation were combined in Mesopotamian ritual practice. The exact purpose of each figurine and aromatic ingredient remains uncertain from this record alone, and the historical procedure must not be treated as a safe modern method.
reflection: What changes when the torch is understood not merely as a flame, but as an assembled object containing figures, aromatics, sulphur, and spoken words?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the phrase I am raising the torch aloud once, then write a short note about how the recorded objects and materials shape your impression of the passage. Do not use fire, smoke, sulphur, plants, or figurines.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. It involves fire, burning sulphur, figurines, and materials that may be toxic, illegal to obtain, or sourced from protected animals.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 27'-30'

title: I Call Upon You: The Sulphur Torch
intro: This lesson examines an early torch rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The rite uses spoken words, a sulphur torch, salt, a tallow figurine, and a vessel in a sequence directed toward evil spoken against the practitioner.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet, in 7th century BC manuscripts, records this rite in the section cited as Tablet IX, with the source citation identifying obv. 6'-13' as a Tablet I section. The incantation begins with the phrase "I call upon you" and is recited three times.

At the line "May that which uttered evil against me", a torch is kindled in burning sulphur. Salt is placed in the mouth of a tallow figurine, which is set on the torch tip so that it drips into a vessel below. When the rite is finished, the torch and vessel are carried out through the entrance, followed by prostration.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the sequence can be understood as joining spoken appeal with the alteration of a figurine through heat, salt, and dripping, then moving the ritual objects outside. The record does not explain every symbol or state exactly what each action was believed to accomplish. Its materials are also described as toxic, illegal to obtain, or sourced from protected animals, so the rite belongs to historical study rather than practice.
reflection: What does the movement from the enclosed ritual space to the entrance suggest to you about how this rite treated the presence of evil spoken against the practitioner?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry aloud without performing any of its actions, then write a short note distinguishing what the source explicitly records from what remains uncertain. Do not gather or use the historical materials.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. It involves flame, burning sulphur, a tallow figurine, and salt, and the record notes materials that may be toxic, illegal to obtain, or sourced from protected animals.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet (Tablet IX) - Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 6'-13' (Tablet I section)

title: Isis Has Spun, Nephthys Has Woven
intro: This lesson examines the first spell for a stung cat in the Metternich Stela. It concerns a bandage described through the divine work of Isis and Nephthys.
body:
The Metternich Stela records this spell in section E, identified as The first spell for a cat. It comes from the Ancient Egyptian tradition and dates to the 30th Dynasty, 4th century BC. The source is the Metternich Stela, held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art as 50.85.

The bandage applied to the animal is described as thread spun by Isis and woven by Nephthys. In this presentation, the physical dressing and the divine act are the same object. Over the bandage, the poison is declared felled and constrained. The speaker affirms that "this bandage shall be strong" and "this magic shall work," then commands the poison, "come, come down!"

What is documented ends there: the text gives the spell's words and its connection between bandage, weaving, and divine power. Read now, this can be understood as a study of how material care and sacred language were joined in the text. It remains uncertain how the spell was understood or used beyond what this record states, and this entry does not establish its medical effectiveness.
reflection: How does the description of Isis spinning and Nephthys weaving change the way you understand the bandage as both a physical object and a spoken act of protection for the cat?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded phrases silently and write a short note about how the bandage is treated as part of the spell. This is a reading and reflection exercise, not a reconstruction and not a treatment for an animal.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Do not use this spell or a bandage in place of modern veterinary or medical care for a stung or poisoned animal.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section E, The first spell for a cat

title: Melt, Dissolve
intro: This lesson examines a capping rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It uses a censer placed over a crucible while the phrase "Melt, dissolve" is recited.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a rite in which the censer standing before Nusku is placed over the opening of a crucible. The instruction is accompanied by the recitation "Melt, dissolve." The source is associated with Mesopotamian, Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition, in manuscripts from the 7th century BC.

The rite's action and words work together in a direct image. Covering the crucible opening smothers the fire, while the spoken phrase names the intended effect. In its own terms, the closing of the vessel and the command to melt or dissolve form a single capping action.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this brief instruction can be understood as a study in how physical closure and concise language were joined in ritual performance. The record does not state what specifically was meant to melt or dissolve, nor does it explain the full intended effect. Any broader interpretation of the target or outcome remains uncertain.
reflection: What might the pairing of a smothered crucible and the words "Melt, dissolve" suggest about the relationship between physical action and spoken intention in this rite?
practice: As a modern practice, place an unlit bowl over a sheet of paper and read the words "Melt, dissolve" aloud as a reflection on letting a difficulty lose its force. Do not use fire, heat, or a hot vessel; this is not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: This historical fire rite is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Do not use live fire or handle hot vessels.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 87'

title: Pure Sulphur, Daughter of the Great Heavens
intro: This lesson examines a sequence of self-identifications from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The practitioner identifies himself with pure sulphur, sulphur linked to the River, and sulphur joined with the holy ataishu plant.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a run of incantations in which the practitioner speaks as sulphur. The sequence begins with "Pure Sulphur, daughter of the great heavens am I," continues with "Sulphur, Sulphur, Sulphur, daughter of River," and ends with "Pure Sulphur and ataishu, the holy plant am I." The record is found in 7th century BC manuscripts of the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition, at obv. 105'-108'.

In its own terms, the working depends on identification. The speaker does not merely address sulphur but presents himself as sulphur, giving it relationships to the great heavens and the River, then pairing it with ataishu. The instruction specifies the use of sulphur at each stage, joining the spoken identities to the named substance.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this sequence can be studied as a focused movement from purity, to a celestial and river connection, to union with a holy plant. It may also invite reflection on how repeated language creates a chosen identity. The record does not explain the precise effect intended by each identification, and that remains uncertain.
reflection: What changes in the sequence when the speaker moves from pure sulphur, to sulphur as the daughter of the River, and then to sulphur joined with ataishu?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the three recorded self-identifications aloud without using sulphur or any plant. Write a brief note about how the repeated naming changes your sense of the speaker's identity.
safetyNote: Burning sulphur produces sulphur dioxide, an acutely hazardous gas. The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 105'-108'

title: River Is My Head, Sulphur My Physique
intro: This lesson examines a passage from the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It describes a full-body identification involving the River, sulphur, and the anhullu and imhurlimu plants.
body:
The passage is preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts of the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, cited at obv. 109'-111'. It records an identification in which the River is named as the head and sulphur as the physique, with the anhullu and imhurlimu plants named alongside. The instruction continues into the phrase River, I have eaten, I have drunk.

In its own terms, the passage presents the body through a series of material identifications. The River is connected with the head, while sulphur and the named plants form part of the physical description. The statements about eating and drinking extend this identification to acts of bodily intake. The record does not provide further explanation of how each material was meant to function.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage can be studied as a compact example of how spoken identification joined a person or body to natural substances. Its language moves between anatomy, materials, and consumption. The purpose and meaning of every named element remain uncertain from this record alone, and no modern effect can be established from it.
reflection: What changes when a body is described not only through its parts, but through a river, sulphur, and plants?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded phrase silently and write a short note on the sequence of identifications: River, sulphur, the two plants, eating, and drinking. Do not handle, burn, or ingest any of the materials.
safetyNote: Burning sulphur produces sulphur dioxide, an acutely hazardous gas. The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 109'-111'

title: Struck Three Times with Cornel
intro: This lesson examines a judicial gesture recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It involves clay figurines, flour likenesses, handwashing, a cornel stick, and the repeated phrase "Huntress of huntresses".
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records two passages in which clay figurines of a warlock and witch are placed on their likenesses drawn in flour. The hands are washed over the figures, and each figure is struck three times with a stick of cornel while "Huntress of huntresses" is recited. The source is represented by 7th century BC manuscripts in the Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition.

In the terms of the record, this is a judicial gesture. The figurines and flour images provide likenesses for the named figures, while washing and repeated striking form the ordered actions. The record gives the sequence and wording, but does not explain further how the gesture was expected to produce its result.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the rite can be studied as a carefully repeated action joining representation, washing, judgment, and the number three. What remains uncertain is the precise meaning of the phrase and the intended force of the gesture within its original setting. The practice note identifies this as a historical reconstruction for study, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What might the combination of likenesses, washing, and three repeated strikes have communicated about judgment to the people who preserved this passage?
practice: As a modern study practice, copy the recorded sequence into a journal and note each action in order. This is for reading and reflection, not a reconstruction of the rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and should not be attempted as a modern rite. The named plant material is part of the ancient record, not a modern prescription.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 143'-147' and 165'-168'

title: The Clay Scorpion on Turquoise
intro: This lesson examines an Ancient Egyptian healing text involving a clay scorpion model, a turquoise base, and a bundle of mn-plants. The rite is recorded in Papyrus Chester Beatty VII and is associated with scorpion danger.
body:
Papyrus Chester Beatty VII records this rite in spells 113 and 112. Dating to the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC, it describes a model rather than a living animal: a clay scorpion set on turquoise with a bundle of mn-plants. Its creation is attributed to Horus, and it is ordered to come forth and break out.

In the text's own terms, the crafted image provided the focus for spoken action. The practitioner identified the model with a making attributed to Horus, then gave it a command. The arrangement of the clay figure, turquoise base, plants, divine attribution, and command formed one connected act.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can show how a model and spoken words were joined in an ancient response to scorpion danger. The record leaves uncertain whether the object was understood mainly as a substitute, a representation, or part of a wider treatment. Its historical value does not make the procedure a safe treatment for a bite or sting.
reflection: What might the choice of a clay scorpion, rather than a living animal, reveal about how this text connected representation with danger and healing?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write a short journal entry about an object that represents a danger you want to understand more clearly. Describe its shape, setting, and the words you would use to acknowledge the danger without directing them at another person.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Bites, stings, and infections are medical emergencies; seek appropriate medical treatment and do not use this text in place of care.
sourceCitation: Papyrus Chester Beatty VII - Borghouts spell 113 (P. Chester Beatty VII, verso 4, 9); spell 112 (verso 4, 4-9)

title: The Faience Lion on Red Linen
intro: This lesson examines a Late Period Egyptian bedroom amulet intended to protect a man by closing the mouth of a snake. The source describes a faience lion threaded onto red linen and applied to the hand after the spell was recited.
body:
The text is identified as Healing statue Cairo JE 69771 and is cited as Borghouts spell 142, with material supplemented by Brooklyn 47.218.89.
